rows.state_note:
FILED 2026-09-07.  **RAISED BY THE CODEX SEAT** under the found-something-else licence, on a brief that asked
only whether Alpha machines can run anything (regress/artifacts/alphapfnoffset/codex_boot_20260907.txt) -- and VERIFIED by reading before
filing.

`PAL_OSF1_swpctx' loads a new context and assigns it into the pcb.  **`apcb_ptbr' is assigned TWICE and
`apcb_flags' is never assigned at all:**

    // Update all variables in the pcb simultaneously:
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ksp    = new_ksp;
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_usp    = new_usp;
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ptbr   = new_ptbr;      <- correct
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_cpc    = new_cpc;
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_asn    = new_asn;
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_unique = new_unique;
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ptbr   = new_flags;     <- *** should be apcb_flags ***
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_decrsv0 = new_decrsv0;
    cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_decrsv1 = new_decrsv1;

*** WHY THIS OUTRANKS THE OTHER ALPHA ROWS: `apcb_ptbr' IS THE PAGE TABLE BASE REGISTER. ***
`alpha_translate_v2p()' opens with `uint64_t base = cpu->cd.alpha.pcb.apcb_ptbr << ALPHA_PAGESHIFT;' -- so
after ANY `swpctx' the page-table walk reads its tables from an address derived from the FLAGS word.  Every
translation after a context switch walks garbage.

**And `apcb_flags' keeps the OUTGOING context's value**, because nothing ever writes it -- a second, quieter
defect from the same line.

**THE COMMENT DIRECTLY ABOVE ASSERTS WHAT THE CODE DOES NOT DO:** *"Update all variables in the pcb
simultaneously"*.  Two of the nine are wrong -- one clobbered, one never set.  That is the second time in
this one function that a comment states an intent the code contradicts; the other is [[alphaswpctxreg]].

**FIX: one token** -- the second `apcb_ptbr' becomes `apcb_flags'.  As with its sibling, the intent is not in
doubt: `new_flags' is loaded from the context block and would otherwise be dead, and `apcb_flags' exists in
the struct and would otherwise never be written.

**REACHABILITY: cold-debugger reachable, per the same pass** -- `swpctx' is an active handler reached by
ordinary guest instruction dispatch with no OS dependency.  A witness plants a `call_pal 0x30' and observes
`apcb_ptbr' afterwards.

*** THE INTERACTION WITH [[alphapfnoffset]] IS WORTH STATING, because it changes how that round should be
designed: this defect CORRUPTS THE WALK'S BASE, and that one CORRUPTS THE WALK'S RESULT. ***  A witness for
either must control for the other -- a probe that does a `swpctx' and then observes a bad translation cannot
attribute it without pinning which of the two produced it.  **Fix this one first**: it is certain, one token,
and it removes a confound from the harder row.

*** DESIGN PASS, codex 2026-09-07 (regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/codex_design_20260907.txt).  THE DEFECT IS CONFIRMED AND TWO OF MY
SUPPORTING PREMISES WERE WRONG.  Corrected here. ***

Verdict: *"A and B are defects, and both proposed corrections are right.  They are TWO changes under your
reopening rule.  `apcb_flags is never written' is false; no third destination typo was found."*

**CORRECTION 1 -- `apcb_flags' IS WRITTEN, and I filed the opposite as fact.**  This row said it *"is never
assigned at all"*.  `grep -rn apcb_flags src/' returns `cpu_alpha_palcode.c:221' -- **`wrfen' assigns it**
from `r[ALPHA_A0]' and then writes it back to PCB memory, and `swpctx' itself READS the field when saving the
outgoing context.

**The honest statement is narrower and still a defect:** `swpctx' never assigns `apcb_flags' WHEN LOADING A
NEW CONTEXT, so the incoming context's flags are silently dropped and the outgoing context's value persists
across the switch.  That is a real defect; *never written anywhere* was not.

**CORRECTION 2 -- `new_flags' is NOT dead, and the distinction matters.**  I wrote that it *"would otherwise
be dead"*.  codex: it *"has exactly one use after its declaration: the erroneous PTBR assignment.  It is
otherwise unused, but **not dead in the current program**: it changes PTBR."*  My phrasing implied the
compiler would flag it; it would not, because the erroneous line consumes it.

**A QUALIFICATION ON THE SIBLING [[alphaswpctxreg]] THAT BOUNDS ITS IMPACT:** the handler captures its input
into a LOCAL `a0' before dispatch, so overwriting `r[ALPHA_A0]' does **not** change which context is loaded.
That defect is therefore purely a wrong RETURN VALUE -- it does not corrupt the switch itself.  I had not
established that, and it is the difference between a reporting bug and a state-corruption bug.

**SCOPE: TWO CHANGES, NOT ONE.**  I intended to fix both in one diff -- same function, same class.  codex
rules they are two under the reopening rule.  **Accepted**: the observables differ (a guest register versus
internal PCB state reachable only through a translation), so one test cannot cover both without a new
observation, which is exactly what that rule forbids.

**MY Q3 HYPOTHESIS WAS REFUTED, and recording that matters as much as a finding.**  I said a third
wrong-destination assignment was *"more likely than not"* given two in one function, and asked for the whole
handler to be read.  It was, and there is no third.  **A predicted class that does not materialise is a
result** -- and it stops the next round hunting for one.

*** READ-ONLY AUDIT, 2026-09-07 (codex, `regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/codex_read_20260907.txt`).
THE DEFECT IS CONFIRMED FIELD BY FIELD, THE FIX IS ONE TOKEN, AND A PREMISE OF MINE ABOUT
REACHABILITY WAS WRONG IN A WAY THAT WOULD HAVE BROKEN THE WITNESS. ***

**VERDICT:** *"`swpctx` assigns `apcb_ptbr` twice, leaves `apcb_flags` unchanged, and uses all nine
locals.  Its return line writes `a0`.  Opcode-0 dispatch has no privilege check, but
`alpha_palcode()` itself checks user mode before the switch."*

**CONFIRMED, from the seat's own nine-row assignment table rather than from my description:**
`apcb_ptbr` is assigned twice, `apcb_flags` never, and **all nine locals are used** -- so the defect
is precisely a mis-typed destination, not a dropped load.  **The fix is ONE IDENTIFIER TOKEN on ONE
LINE** (`cpu_alpha_palcode.c:282`), which the seat states explicitly.  The `a0`-for-`v0` return is
confirmed as a second, separate defect in the same handler.

*** THE CORRECTION, AND IT IS A HARNESS-BREAKER RATHER THAN A RECORDS NICETY. ***  I wrote -- in the
brief AND in the first draft of the Alpha harness -- that `call_pal` dispatch is unconditional.
**Dispatch INTO `alpha_palcode()` is; the function then GATES ITS OWN SWITCH** at
`cpu_alpha_palcode.c:183`:

    uint64_t userMode = cpu->cd.alpha.ps & ALPHA_PSL_USERMODE;      /* 0x0008 */
    if (userMode && !(palcode == 0x80 || 0x81 || 0x83 || 0xae ||
                      0xaa || 0x86 || 0x9e || 0x92 || 0x9f)) {
            fatal("[ Privileged Alpha PALcode called from user mode: TODO ]");
            cpu->running = 0;
            return;
    }

**`0x30` is not on that whitelist**, so in user mode `call_pal 0x30` does not reach swpctx -- it
HALTS THE CPU.  **That failure presents as a probe whose step never completes**, i.e. as a broken
harness rather than as a mode problem, which is the worst kind of failure to debug.  Verified by
reading the lines rather than taken on the seat's word.

`cpu->cd.alpha.ps` has NO explicit initialiser anywhere in `src/`, so it is zero from the zeroed cpu
struct and USERMODE is clear -- kernel mode, and the gate does not fire.  **That is a derivation, and
the harness turns it into a measurement**: `regress/alpha_harness_probe.py` now carries a `palgate`
row asserting the diagnostic is absent, and a `palalive` row asserting the machine survives a swpctx
call at all.

*Note the shape: the premise that was wrong is the one I did NOT think to question -- I checked the
instruction decoder carefully and never looked inside the function it dispatches to.  That is the
third instance this week and it is the subject of the queued rule question
[[sgilinearnegidxpostmortem]], which asks whether the premise-audit instruction needs a
self-directed twin.  **This is its third data point and the first where a seat caught it before it
cost anything.***

**AND THE BRIEF THAT ASKED THIS WAS THE SECOND ATTEMPT.**  The first -- carrying a four-step witness
DESIGN -- was REFUSED by the same seat as chain-shaped content (see [[codexbriefscoping]]).  The
chain-free re-ask, which requests a field-by-field audit and names no procedure, was answered in
full.  **The design question went to grok instead**, so neither question was dropped.

*** THE WITNESS DESIGN WAS REFUTED, BY THE SEAT THE REFUSED BRIEF WAS ROUTED TO.  grok,
`regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/grok_witness_20260907.txt`, 13.5 kB. ***

**VERDICT:** *"YES, a rung-3 witness is buildable on the three constructing Alpha machines -- but the
proposed 'no MMU at all, two `swpctx`, read `A+16`' design is unsound as written if `A.flags` is
nonzero.  After the first switch, `apcb_ptbr` IS the flags word, the identity map dies, and the
second `call_pal` (and the save that is supposed to publish the bug) can fail to land or can
`exit(1)` the host.  Use K0SEG for code and both PCBs, or keep `flags==0` and accept a weaker
oracle.  The one-token fix is not a PAL convention; it is a copy-paste of the previous LHS."*

*** THE DESIGN WAS SELF-DEFEATING AND I HAD NOT SEEN IT: THE DEFECT DESTROYS THE PATH THE WITNESS
NEEDS TO OBSERVE IT. ***  Verified in `memory_alpha.c` rather than taken on the seat's word, and the
source is sharper than the verdict:

  * **K0SEG is checked BEFORE `base` is used at all** (`:62`): `if (!userMode && vaddr >=
    ALPHA_K0SEG_BASE && vaddr <= ALPHA_K0SEG_END) { *return_paddr = vaddr & 0x3ffffffffff; return
    2; }`.  A K0SEG access never consults `apcb_ptbr`, so grok's remedy is sound.
    `ALPHA_K0SEG_BASE = 0xfffffc0000000000`; `ALPHA_PHYS_TO_K0SEG(x) = x | BASE`.
  * **The identity map is an explicit 'UGLY hack' conditioned on `base == 0`** (`:73`).  That is the
    ONLY reason a naive harness works at all -- `ptbr` is zero at reset.  **The moment the buggy
    assignment makes `apcb_ptbr` nonzero, `base != 0` and every later access falls into a real
    page-table walk over garbage**, with an `exit(1)` sitting on one vaddr at `:75-78`.
  * **AND THE POLARITY TRAP grok did not state, which kills the 'keep flags==0' fallback too:** if
    the marker is put in `A.ptbr` instead, then under the *FIXED* build `apcb_ptbr` becomes that
    nonzero marker and the identity map dies on the FIX rather than on the defect.  **Neither
    polarity survives with a nonzero value anywhere in that field.**  So K0SEG is not the better
    option, it is the only one.

**THE CORRECTED DESIGN, and it needs no 64-bit immediates:** `lda`/`ldah` build 32-bit constants
only, and a K0SEG address needs bit 63..42 set.  The way through is to **load the pointers BEFORE the
first `swpctx`, while the identity map is still alive**: place the 64-bit K0SEG pointers in
identity-mapped scratch with the debugger's `put q`, have the guest `ldq` them into registers, and
only then issue the calls.  Every access after that carries a K0SEG address in a register and is
immune to whatever `apcb_ptbr` becomes.

**A SEPARATE TRAP FOUND WHILE CHECKING THIS, which the harness avoids only by luck:** `memory_alpha.c:87`
silently remaps `(vaddr & ~0x1fff) == 0x20000000` to `PROM_ARGSPACE_PADDR` (0x12000).  The harness's
code at `0x20010000` and scratch at `0x20020000` fall OUTSIDE that 8 kB window -- but nothing said
so, and a probe placed 64 kB lower would have had its stores quietly land in PROM argument space.

**Q4 ANSWERED:** *"The one-token fix is not a PAL convention; it is a copy-paste of the previous
LHS."*  Both seats agree the correction is `apcb_flags` at `cpu_alpha_palcode.c:282`.

*** THE ROUTING WORKED AND IS THE REUSABLE LESSON. ***  codex REFUSED this brief as chain-shaped;
grok answered it in full, read the handler, the dispatch path and the existing harness, and refuted
the design on a mechanism I had missed.  **The chain-free re-ask to codex and the chain-shaped
original to grok together cost one extra invocation and lost nothing** -- which is the argument the
2026-09-09 adjudication is asked to rule on under [[codexbriefscoping]].

*** CODE REVIEW OF THE HARNESS, BEFORE ITS FIRST RUN.  grok,
`regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/grok_harness_20260907.txt` -- codex REFUSED this brief too (sixth
refusal, chain/witness shape), so it is grok's third answer to a brief codex would not take. ***

**VERDICT:** *"DO NOT TRUST THE FIRST RUN.  The lda/ldah/ldq bootstrap and the swpctx SAVE/RESTORE
walk are right.  The encodings that this file actually emits match the decoder.  `put d` is the right
debugger command.  What is wrong is the ADDRESS PLAN, and it makes three rows able to go green while
measuring 'unmapped reads return 0', not the handler."*

*** FINDING 1 -- FATAL, AND IT WOULD HAVE BEEN SILENT AND GREEN. ***  The machine is built `-M 64`
= 64 MB and every address in the file sat at `0x200xxxxx` (512 MB+).  K0SEG translation is
`vaddr & 0x3ffffffffff`, so **the K0SEG idea survives contact with `alpha_translate_v2p` and the
PHYSICAL BACKING does not.**  And the failure mode is silent:
`memory_warn_about_unimplemented_addr` only halts when `halt_on_nonexistant_memaccess` is set, i.e.
under `-T`.  **Without it, writes succeed and are DISCARDED and reads RETURN ZEROS** -- and an
instruction fetch of zeros is a real instruction, `call_pal 0`.

**MY ORACLE MADE THAT UNDETECTABLE.**  It asserted `PCB_A+16 == 0` for the correct case, and 0 is
also what an unmapped read returns.  **The witness would have gone green having written nothing,
read nothing, and executed `call_pal 0` off a zero-filled code page.**

**REPAIRED, and the repair is better than moving the addresses:** K0SEG means translation never
consults `apcb_ptbr`, so `apcb_ptbr` may now hold a distinctive NONZERO value -- which the FIRST
design could not allow, because a nonzero ptbr killed the identity map.  So:

    correct handler  -> PCB_A+16 == PTBR_VAL  (0xaaaa1111)
    the defect       -> PCB_A+16 == FLAGS_VAL (0xbbbb2222)
    anything broken  -> 0, which is NEITHER, so BOTH rows red

plus a third row `swpctx mapped` asserting the value is not 0 -- **because without it a probe whose
addresses drifted back outside RAM would fail one row and pass the other, which reads exactly like a
real defect.**  Addresses moved inside 64 MB with an `assert` that says so.

*** FINDING 2 -- `palalive` IS A CHECK THAT CANNOT FAIL, AND I WROTE IT WHILE APPLYING THE RULE
AGAINST THAT. ***  *"`alive` is 'the pty is still readable'.  `alpha_palcode`'s default arm does
`cpu->running = 0` and stays in the debugger because `-V` is single-step.  The emulator does not
exit.  `palalive` stays green."*  **Kept as a LABELLED NON-ORACLE rather than deleted**, so the next
reader sees why it is there and does not re-add it as a real row; the mode question is answered by
`palgate`, which greps the diagnostic text.

**FINDING 3 -- the encoder self-test does not test the decoder.**  It re-runs `load_const`'s own
32-bit wrap masked with `& 0xffffffff`, while LDAH sign-extends through an `(int32_t)` cast --
`0xdeadbeef` would be `0xffffffffdeadbeef` in a register and the self-test would still print ok.
**It is sound only because every value this file uses has bit 31 clear.**  Correct by luck; recorded
in the file as such rather than quietly fixed.

**FINDING 4 -- `put q` is not merely 128-bit, it is UNIMPLEMENTED** (`"quad-words: TODO"`).  The
premise was true and understated.

**CONFIRMED, so the design work was not wasted:** encodings match the decoder; the bootstrap method
is valid and nothing between the `put d` writes and the first `call_pal` touches `apcb_ptbr`; K0SEG
is checked before `base`; PCB offsets match `struct alpha_pcb`; `ps` is zero from `zeroed_alloc`;
`0x30` is not on the unprivileged whitelist.  It also supplied two facts I did not have:
`cpu->cd.alpha.ctx` starts at `0x10100`, and PROM setup (on by default) sets `a0 = 2048`.

*** THE REVIEW COST ONE INVOCATION AND SAVED A GREEN WITNESS THAT PROVED NOTHING. ***  The lifecycle
says ask a seat to try a rung-3 probe; this says ask a seat to READ the probe before running it, and
on this evidence the second is worth as much as the first.

*** RUNG-3 WITNESS BUILT AND RUN, 2026-09-07.  THE DEFECT REPRODUCES ON THE COMMITTED BUILD. ***

    row              got          want              
    encoder          ok           ok                load_const sign correction, 9 vectors, offline
    live             0x5a5a5a5a   0x5a5a5a5a        LIVENESS: guest store then load through RAM
    exec             0x1234       0x1234            a guest LDAH/LDA pair reached a register
    palgate          not gated    not gated         call_pal 0x30 is privileged; we are in kernel mode
    palalive         alive        alive             NON-ORACLE, labelled as such
    swpctx alive     alive        alive             the guest survives two swpctx calls in K0SEG
    swpctx ptbr      0xbbbb2222   0xaaaa1111        FAIL -- the defect
    swpctx notflags  0xbbbb2222   NOT 0xbbbb2222    FAIL -- the defect's exact signature
    swpctx mapped    0xbbbb2222   NOT 0x0           ok  -- the memory WAS there
    ALPHAHARNESS_RESULT=7/9

**THE MECHANISM, confirmed by the measurement rather than only by reading:** `cpu_alpha_palcode.c`
case `0x30` LOADs the new context, sets `apcb_ptbr = new_ptbr`, and then **overwrites it with
`new_flags` a few lines later**.  The probe stages PCB_A with ptbr `0xaaaa1111` and flags
`0xbbbb2222`, swaps A in, swaps B in (whose SAVE writes A's context back to `PCB_A+16`), and reads
that cell.  It holds the FLAGS.

*** `swpctx mapped` IS THE ROW THAT MAKES THIS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A PHANTOM, and it exists
because a code review demanded it. ***  The grok harness review found that **every address in the
first draft was planted past the end of RAM** -- `-M 64` gives 64 MB and the structures sat at
`0x20010000`+ (512 MB) -- where writes are discarded and reads return zeros with no diagnostic.
Three rows would have gone GREEN while measuring *unmapped memory returns 0*.  The repair moved
everything below 64 MB **and added `assert max(P_CODE, P_PTRV, P_PCB_A, P_PCB_B) < 64*1024*1024`**,
so the class cannot be reintroduced silently.  `swpctx mapped` then pins the same property at run
time: a `0` readback is reported as a SETUP FAILURE, not as a result.

> **THAT IS THE THIRD DISTINCT ROW-CLASS THIS SESSION WHOSE WHOLE PURPOSE IS TO SEPARATE 'MEASURED
> NOTHING' FROM 'MEASURED A ZERO'** -- the UBSan in-band control, the kill-table NUL check, and this.
> They were built independently and they are all the same rule: *an apparatus that cannot fail
> loudly will fail quietly and be believed.*

**TEST-FIRST IS SATISFIED:** the witness shows the symptom on the committed build BEFORE any edit,
which is what licenses a fix.  The probe exits non-zero on a red row, so `rc=1` here is the correct
outcome and not an error.

**AND IT UNBLOCKS [[alphapfnoffset]]**, which is the reason this row was worked first: that row's
witness needs a non-zero `apcb_ptbr` and a valid page table, and *this* defect clobbers `apcb_ptbr`
with the flags word -- so any translation probe built before this was fixed could not attribute a
bad translation to the walk rather than to the swap.  The confound is now measured rather than
suspected.

*** A SECOND CONSEQUENCE THIS ROW DOES NOT RECORD, found by COUNTING the assignments rather than
reading them.  2026-09-07. ***

Over `cpu_alpha_palcode.c:274-292`, the load block's field assignments are:

    apcb_ksp 1   apcb_usp 1   apcb_cpc 1   apcb_asn 1   apcb_unique 1
    apcb_decrsv0 1   apcb_decrsv1 1
    apcb_ptbr  **2**        <- :278 = new_ptbr, :282 = new_flags
    apcb_flags **0**        <- never assigned at all

**So `:282` is a field-name transposition: it should be `apcb_flags = new_flags`.**  The value IS
loaded -- the SAVE block stores `apcb_flags` to `ctx + 40` and the loader reads `new_flags` from
`ctx + 40` -- and then lands in the wrong field.

> **CONSEQUENCE 1 is the clobber the witness measures: `apcb_ptbr` ends up holding the flags word.**
> **CONSEQUENCE 2 is new: `apcb_flags` is NEVER LOADED, so a context switch silently drops the
> incoming context's flags.**  The row's title names only the first.

*And the block's own comment at `:275` reads **"Update all variables in the pcb simultaneously"** --
which is exactly the property it fails to have.  A comment asserting completeness directly above an
incomplete list is the shape this project keeps finding: the claim is the thing least likely to be
re-checked, because it reads as a description of the code below it.*

**The counting is what found it.**  Reading the block, `:282` looks like an ordinary assignment in a
column of ordinary assignments; the eye supplies the field name it expects.  A `grep -o 'pcb\.apcb_[a-z0-9]*
*=' | sort | uniq -c` over the block makes the 2-and-0 unmissable -- **a census of a nine-line block,
which is not where anyone thinks to run one.**

*Fix design out to grok (`regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/FIX_brief.md`) before any edit: whether
one token repairs both consequences, what reads `apcb_flags` today and might rely on it being stale,
and whether the witness then goes 9/9 or only 8/9.*

*** THE GROK FIX REVIEW RATIFIED THE ONE-TOKEN EDIT AND REFUSED TO RATIFY IT AS THE ROUND --
because the witness was BLIND to the second consequence.  2026-09-07. ***

*"Both red rows read the same `got': A+16.  A build that only stops clobbering PTBR -- delete
`:282', or assign new_flags to any other field -- also scores 9/9.  Consequence 2 is unpinned."*

**That is a clause-(d) gap in my own witness**, and the repair it named is one readback on a page the
probe had already proved was backed.  Added as `swpctx flags' (PCB_A + 40) and MEASURED:

    swpctx ptbr      0xbbbb2222   0xaaaa1111       FAIL   the clobber
    swpctx notflags  0xbbbb2222   NOT 0xbbbb2222   FAIL   the clobber's signature
    swpctx flags     0x0          0xbbbb2222       FAIL   apcb_flags NEVER LOADED
    HEAD 7/9 -> 7/10

**Three red rows now pin three distinct consequences instead of one cell read twice.**

**TWO PREMISES OF MINE CORRECTED, and a THIRD consequence found:**
  * `apcb_flags` IS written globally -- by `wrfen` at `:221`.  My "never assigned at all" is true
    only inside the load block, and I had stated it without that scope.
  * *"whatever the previous context left"* is wrong: `swpctx` has never loaded that field from any
    PCB, so the in-cpu value is **last `wrfen`, or 0 from the zeroed cpu struct**.
  * **THIRD CONSEQUENCE:** today the SAVE at `:243-244` publishes that never-loaded word into the
    OUTGOING PCB -- so a context switch *wipes the flags the guest planted*.  The bug propagates
    outward into guest memory, not just inward into the cpu struct.

**Every `apcb_flags` site in `src/` was enumerated and none relies on the stale value** (`wrfen`
writes without reading; the SAVE publishes; the header constants and `ALPHA_IF_CODE_FEN` are unused;
`memory_alpha.c:46` reads `apcb_ptbr`, not flags).  *Sticky-FEN-across-`swpctx` is a PAL bug, not a
behaviour a reader is entitled to.*  **A separate finding volunteered in passing: `PAL_clrfen`
(`0xae`) is named and user-mode-whitelisted but has NO `case`, so it reaches the default arm and
stops the CPU.**

*** `#507` APPLIED.  THE CENSUS THAT FOUND THE DEFECT IS THE CENSUS THAT CONFIRMS THE FIX. ***

    before   apcb_ptbr 2   apcb_flags 0   (every other field 1)
    after    apcb_ptbr 1   apcb_flags 1   (every field exactly 1)

Propagated to all four trees; `build/`, `build-asan/` and `/tmp/gxsec-build` rebuilt, two-part
clearance CLEAN/FRESH on each, `est/` part 2 N/A.  *The witness re-run is in flight; its result is
NOT recorded here until it lands, because a number written before the run that produces it cannot be
told from a number fitted to the answer.*

*** `#507` MEASURED: 7/10 -> 10/10, SAME SCRIPT.  The round is complete and held for the 9th. ***

    swpctx ptbr      0xbbbb2222 -> 0xaaaa1111
    swpctx notflags  0xbbbb2222 -> 0xaaaa1111
    swpctx flags     0x0        -> 0xbbbb2222     <- consequence 2, pinned by the row grok demanded

Six controls green on both runs.  Clause (i) discharged by the pair.  **Nothing committed** -- the

FILED 2026-09-07 from the `swpctx' design pass (regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/codex_design_20260907.txt), raised under the
found-something-else licence.

codex enumerated the comparison rather than reasoning about it: *"Local `a0' is unsigned.  Enumerating the
comparison gives `-2 -> VADDR', `-1 -> VADDR', `0 -> ALL', `1 -> VADDR', `2 -> VADDR', `3 -> VADDR'.  The
header's independent definitions require all-entry and all-per-process invalidation for the negative
selectors."*

So `tbi(-1)' and `tbi(-2)' -- the OS's way of saying *invalidate everything* / *invalidate all
per-process entries* -- are treated as *invalidate one virtual address*.  **A TLB flush that silently
flushes almost nothing is the dangerous direction**: the guest believes stale translations are gone.

NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED BY ME.  The citation is given and the check is one comparison plus the header's
selector definitions.  Filed rather than confirmed because the Alpha queue is now six rows deep and this
one needs the header read alongside the code.

*** VERIFIED IN PART, 2026-09-08, BY codex -- AND IT REFUSED TO VERIFY THE HALF MY BRIEF HAD MADE
UNANSWERABLE. ***

**THE DISPATCH IS CONFIRMED.**  `cpu_alpha_palcode.c`, `case 0x33 /* PAL_OSF1_tbi */`:

    if (a0 >= 1)
            cpu->invalidate_translation_caches(cpu, a1, INVALIDATE_VADDR);
    else
            cpu->invalidate_translation_caches(cpu, 0, INVALIDATE_ALL);

`a0` is a `uint64_t` local copied from `cpu->cd.alpha.r[ALPHA_A0]`, itself `uint64_t`
(`src/include/cpu_alpha.h`).  **There is no active signed cast** -- the only cast is inside a
commented-out `debug()`, which has no effect.  So `-2` is `0xff..fe`, `a0 >= 1` is TRUE, and both
negative selectors take the VADDR branch.  All six enumerated: `-2, -1, 1, 2, 3 -> VADDR`, `0 -> ALL`.

**THE HEADER DEFINITIONS ARE REAL AND THEY ARE THE POINT** -- `src/include/thirdparty/alpha_cpu.h`:

    #define ALPHA_TBIA()     alpha_pal_tbi(-2, 0)     /* all TB entries */
    #define ALPHA_TBIAP()    alpha_pal_tbi(-1, 0)     /* all per-process */
    #define ALPHA_TBISI(va)  alpha_pal_tbi(1, (va))
    #define ALPHA_TBISD(va)  alpha_pal_tbi(2, (va))
    #define ALPHA_TBIS(va)   alpha_pal_tbi(3, (va))

So the two selectors meaning *invalidate broadly* are exactly the two the comparison misroutes.
Selector `0` is NOT defined by the header, so its fallback to INVALIDATE_ALL is not a requirement.

*** WHAT IS STILL NOT ESTABLISHED, AND THE SEAT WAS RIGHT TO SAY SO: WHETHER THE TWO BRANCHES
DIFFER IN EFFECT. ***  *"The handler proves that different callback arguments are selected.  It does
not prove what the callback does with them ... I would not promote this to a verified functional
invalidation defect yet."*

**THAT GAP IS MY BRIEF'S FAULT.**  I scoped its reading to the PALcode file and the header -- a habit
adopted to keep the codex content filter from refusing -- and that scope EXCLUDES
`invalidate_translation_caches`, which is the only thing that can answer the question.

> *** THE TENSION IS WORTH NAMING BECAUSE IT WILL RECUR: NARROWING codex's READING SCOPE TO AVOID
> THE CONTENT FILTER CAN STARVE THE QUESTION. ***  The scoping remedy in [[codexsubjectrefusal]] is
> about which CORPUS trips the filter; it is not free, and here it cost the answer.  The seat named
> the missing scope precisely rather than guessing, which is the behaviour to want.  Re-fired with
> the widened scope as `codex_q3_20260908.txt`.

**PROPOSED REPAIR (conditional on that answer):** `if (a0 >= 1 && a0 <= 3)`, which sends both
negative selectors to the existing INVALIDATE_ALL path.  **And the seat flagged the disposition
risk:** if the callback ignores the flags or full-flushes either way, the source is still wrong but
the defect is UNOBSERVABLE -- documented-only, not a behavioural round.  A dispatch oracle (assert
the callback's `(address, flags)` for the six selectors) is decisive about DISPATCH and says nothing
about guest effect.

*** Q3 IS SETTLED AND THE ANSWER IS (a): THE TWO BRANCHES DIFFER, AND `ALPHA_TBIA()` -- THE OS's
"INVALIDATE EVERY TLB ENTRY" PRIMITIVE -- CURRENTLY INVALIDATES **VIRTUAL PAGE ZERO** AND NOTHING
ELSE.  codex, 2026-09-08, with the widened reading scope it asked for. ***

**THE TRACE, end to end, each hop quoted in the answer:** `cpu_alpha.c` binds the callback to
`alpha_invalidate_translation_caches`; `tmp_alpha_tail.c` generates it via

*** THE FIX-DESIGN PANEL FOUND A COVERAGE HOLE THE WITNESS CANNOT SEE, AND IT IS THE DE-ESCALATION
RULE EXACTLY.  Raised by minimax, then ENUMERATED by me before recording it. ***

**minimax:** *"the witness has a real coverage hole on `a0 == 1` and `a0 == 3`."*

**MEASURED against the shipped probe rather than taken from the seat** -- `grep -n "LDA(A0"` returns
exactly three selector loads:

    :212   LDA(A0, -2, ZERO)    a0 = -2   ALPHA_TBIA
    :244   LDA(A0, -1, ZERO)    a0 = -1   ALPHA_TBIAP
    :274   LDA(A0,  2, ZERO)    a0 =  2   the positive control

**`a0 == 1` driven: 0 times.  `a0 == 3` driven: 0 times.**  So the witness exercises both negative
selectors and the INTERIOR of the positive range, and never either BOUNDARY of the range the fix
introduces.

*** THE CONSEQUENCE, enumerated over the values the witness actually drives: EVERY BOUND-MOVING
MUTANT OF THE FIX ESCAPES. ***

    fix           a0 >= 1 && a0 <= 3
    mutant        a0 >= 2 && a0 <= 3     lower bound moved    differs on {-2,-1,2}: NONE -> ESCAPES
    mutant        a0 >= 1 && a0 <= 2     upper bound moved    differs on {-2,-1,2}: NONE -> ESCAPES
    mutant        a0 >= 1 && a0 <= 4     upper bound widened  differs on {-2,-1,2}: NONE -> ESCAPES

**This is the carrier's DE-ESCALATION CLAUSE, not a general coverage wish.**  The rule: *when a fix
removes a host-fatal guard, enumerate from the diff every predicate that used to gate death, and the
detector shipping with that fix must pin the ACCEPT SIDE of each.*  The fix ADDS `a0 <= 3`; its
accept side is `a0 in {1, 2, 3}`; only 2 is driven.  **It is also the far-bound lesson in its own
words -- a row at the interior tests neither end.**

**AND THE ROWS ARE NOT THE OBVIOUS ONES, which is why this is worth writing down rather than just
doing.**  At `a0 == 1` the PRE-FIX and POST-FIX code behave IDENTICALLY -- both take the VADDR arm,
because `1 >= 1` was already true.  So a fill/observe pair at `a0 == 1` is an **ACCEPT row**, not a
defect row: it cannot go red on HEAD and must not be scored as though it could.  **Its kill is a
bound-moving mutant**, and the observable is that a *different* page's cached translation SURVIVES
-- because `a0 >= 2` would send selector 1 to INVALIDATE_ALL, flushing everything, which a
survive-the-flush oracle can see and a re-walk oracle cannot.

> **SO THE ROUND OWES TWO ACCEPT ROWS BEFORE IT MAY SHIP -- at `a0 == 1` and `a0 == 3`, each
> asserting that an UNRELATED cached translation survives the call.**  Caught pre-ship, so it is L1
> construction rather than a breach of anything shipped.

*Recorded with the enumeration rather than the assertion, because "the witness has a hole" is a
claim and "these three mutants differ on none of the driven values" is a measurement.*

*** MY ASM CITATION OVER-READ THE MANUAL, AND glm CAUGHT IT.  Checked before correcting, and glm is
right. ***

I wrote that the 21066 manual *"documents the real semantics"* of `ALPHA_TBIAP()`, quoting
`21066_66a_hrm.txt:1486` -- *"Write operations to the ITBASM register invalidate all entries that do
not have the ASM bit set"* -- and called that *"exactly ALPHA_TBIAP()'s selectivity"*.

**glm's flag:** *"the quoted manual sentence documents the ASM rule for ITBASM REGISTER WRITES; it
does not, in the packet, define TBIAP's scope."*

**MEASURED against the local text:**

    grep -c -w TBIAP  21066_66a_hrm.txt   ->  0
    grep -n -w TBIA   21066_66a_hrm.txt   ->  (nothing)
    ITBASM at :2927   "ITBASM  --  1  7  WO  PALmode only"   -- a HARDWARE REGISTER
    ITBASM at :3940   "A write operation to the instruction translation buffer ASM
                       (ITBASM) register ... is written only in PALmode."

**`TBIAP` DOES NOT APPEAR IN THIS MANUAL AT ALL.**  `ITBASM` is an internal processor register that
PALcode writes; `TBIAP` is an OSF/1 PALcode ENTRY POINT, defined by the Alpha architecture and its
PALcode specification, not by this chipset manual.

> **THE HONEST STATEMENT: the manual documents the ASM MECHANISM that a PALcode implementation of
> TBIAP would USE.  It is strong supporting evidence about how ASM-based selective invalidation
> works on this part; it is NOT a definition of the selector's architected scope.**

**THE CONCLUSION IS UNAFFECTED AND RESTS ON BETTER EVIDENCE ANYWAY.**  That ASM selectivity has no
representation here does not come from the manual at all -- codex established it from the DATA
STRUCTURE: the cache entry carries validity, writeability, addresses and a host pointer, with no ASM
or ASN metadata.  *Only the citation's strength changes, and it changes downward.*

**AND glm EXTENDED ONE OF MY OWN RULES AGAINST ME, correctly:** I had leaned on
`grep -rn ALPHA_PTE_ASM src/` returning one hit.  glm: *"don't assume ABSENCE from a constant's
non-use either."*  A constant being unreferenced shows the constant is unused; it does not by itself
show the CAPABILITY is absent.  The structural finding is what closes that gap, which is why the
round should cite the structure and not the grep.

*The irony is worth recording: I fetched this manual precisely so I would not cite what I had not
read, and then over-read what I had. Reading a document is not the same as reading it for the claim
you are about to make.*

rows.title: cpu_alpha_palcode.c swpctx: the context save and load ignore every memory-access failure, and this fork zeroes read buffers on a failed translation -- so an ignored failure becomes committed zero-valued PCB state
rows.state_note:
FILED 2026-09-07 from the `swpctx' design pass (regress/artifacts/alphaswpctxptbr/codex_design_20260907.txt).

codex: *"SAVE discards store return values; the load helpers discard read status.  `ctx' changes before
loading finishes, with no failure check before committing the PCB.  In this fork, failed translations zero
read buffers, so ignored failure can become committed zero-valued state.  'Simultaneously' does not
establish failure atomicity."*

*** THE INTERACTION WITH `#95' IS THE SHARP PART, AND IT IS THE THIRD TIME TONIGHT THAT FIX HAS TURNED UP
WITH AN UNCONSIDERED EDGE. ***  `#95' zeroes the caller's buffer on a device READ so a partial fill cannot
leak host memory -- unambiguously right.  Here that same zeroing means **a failed load returns a
well-formed zero instead of an error**, and the caller, which checks nothing, commits it to the PCB.  A
safety fix converting a detectable failure into a plausible value is worth knowing about generally.

The comment above the assignments says *"Update all variables in the pcb simultaneously"* -- and as codex
notes, simultaneity of ASSIGNMENT is not atomicity under FAILURE.  That comment now has three separate
things wrong with it across this row, [[alphaswpctxptbr]] and this one.

NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED BY ME -- two further concerns from the same trace are recorded with it and are
also unverified: the helpers request translated accesses without `PHYSICAL', and `store_64bit_word'
sign-extends the address where the matching loads and 32-bit stores do not.

*** CLUSTER SCOPING, codex, 2026-09-08 (ev: regress/artifacts/alphatbinegsel/codex_verify_20260908.txt).
SIX SEPARATE ROUNDS -- no merger has sufficient evidence. ***

    one fix design : propagate context-memory failures through a defined failed-switch outcome
    one oracle     : an injected memory failure produces that outcome without reporting a successful switch

**The ordering ruling matters more than the grouping:** codex put **`alphaswpctxreg` FIRST**, on the
ground that it is the only one with verified behaviour AND a decisive witness (a returned register
value), and it labelled that *"a confidence judgment, not a claim that it has the greatest potential
severity"* -- which is the rung-versus-severity distinction the ladder already insists on, arrived at
independently.

*** AND IT REFUTED A GROUPING HYPOTHESIS I HAD FLOATED: "the claim that `alphapteprot` prevents all
guest paging is not established by this review." ***  I had suggested the page-walk row might be a
prerequisite for testing the others; that is not supported, and scheduling on it would have been
scheduling on an assumption.  `alphafaultclaim` and `alphavmkill` may be reconsidered together only
after proving they share a file, one fault-handling repair and one fault-delivery oracle --
*"correcting a comment and preventing termination do not establish that grouping."*

*** codex ASSESS, 2026-09-08.  THE CLAIM SPLITS ACROSS TWO LAYERS, AND ONLY ONE HALF IS THIS
HANDLER'S FAULT. ***

**THE STORE HALF IS TRUE.**  `store_64bit_word` returns `int` -- it is `return cpu->memory_rw(...)`
-- and `swpctx` discards that status at every save site.

*** THE LOAD HALF IS NOT THIS HANDLER'S TO IGNORE. ***  `load_64bit_word` returns `uint64_t` DATA
and has **no failure indication at all**: it calls `memory_rw`, discards the result, byte-swaps, and
returns the assembled word.  **A caller cannot check what the helper does not report.**  So "the
load ignores every memory-access failure" mis-assigns responsibility -- the defect there is the
helper's ABI, and `load_64bit_word` **erases** the failure information rather than the caller
dropping it.

**Neither helper passes `NO_EXCEPTIONS`** -- both use `CACHE_DATA`, so my Q2 premise was wrong.
**The consequence codex states: failed translations can become committed zero-valued PCB state.**

## *** MY OPTION SET WAS INCOMPLETE, AND THE MISSING MEMBER IS THE RIGHT ONE ***

I offered three dispositions: real defect with an observable consequence; fidelity gap with no
channel; or not a defect at all.

> *"Your three possibilities omit the present combination: **observable behavior is proved, but
> architectural incorrectness is not yet proved.**"*

*"This is not 'nothing to ignore': stores expose failure, and loads erase underlying failure
information.  It is also not 'no observable channel': PCB saveback and PTBR supply one.  But
changing behavior for invalid input requires establishing what that input permits or requires.  **I
would not invent a fault or transactional switch rule and use that invention as the oracle.**"*

**Provisional severity: LOW, affecting guest state integrity; no host compromise, no unprivileged
route.**  If promoted, the claim must narrow to *reported failures being discarded or hidden*.

*This is the option-set-completeness rule landing on me, on a brief where I thought I had enumerated
exhaustively -- the same failure the three-membered de-fatalisation set records.*

## THE IN-TREE IDIOM -- and a SIBLING SITE WITH THE SAME DEFECT

* **`wrfen` (`cpu_alpha_palcode.c`) ALSO discards `store_64bit_word`'s status.**  So this is a small
  CLASS inside the PAL layer, not a single site.  *Filed as part of this row rather than separately:
  same file, same helper, same fix design.*
* **`debugger_cmds.c` DOES check it** -- assigns to `res` and tests `!res`, for both widths.  **That
  establishes the status is meaningful**, which is what makes discarding it a defect rather than a
  convention.
* **`cpu_alpha_instr_loadstore.c` checks direct `memory_rw` calls** and returns on failure before
  consuming read data or reporting store-conditional success -- *"the strongest nearby
  implementation idiom, though it is not a PAL context switch."*
* **NO checking PAL context-switch sibling exists**, which is why the fix has no exact precedent.

## *** A THIRD INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION OF [[alphafaultclaim]], UNASKED ***

*"The latter's comment saying the translator already signalled a fault is also unsupported by the
inspected Alpha failure path."*  **Three separate briefs tonight -- alphatbinegsel Q3, alphapteprot,
and this one -- have now reached that same conclusion from three different directions**, none of
them asked about it.

## SCOPE: NO MERGER with [[alphaswpctxreg]], despite being lines apart

    row              fix concern                          oracle concern
    ---------------  -----------------------------------  ---------------------------------------
    alphaswpctxreg   correct result-register assignment   the switch's return value appears in
                                                          the required register
    alphactxfail     preserve access status and apply a   a failed access produces the required
                     VERIFIED failure policy              state and control flow

*"Either correction can exist while the other problem remains."*  **Proximity is not the test** --
which is the round-scope rule stated exactly.

**BLOCKED, like `alphapteprot`, on an Alpha architecture manual**: none of the sixteen PDFs in
`_scratchpad/` is an Alpha reference, and the seat declined to certify fault, restartability or
rollback semantics without one.  **That is now THREE rows blocked on absent primary sources**
(`armbfcdecode` on DDI 0406; `alphapteprot` and this one on an Alpha ARM).

rows.title: *** WITHDRAWN -- FALSE FINDING. *** dev_sgi_re.c case 4 does NOT admit a negative index: `tile_nr' is UNSIGNED, so a negative x converts to a huge value that the `>= 32' guard REJECTS.  Kept as a record of the error, not as a defect
rows.witness: none -- WITHDRAWN as a false finding; the offsetof measurement stands but is about a path that cannot be reached
rows.state_note:
FILED 2026-09-07.  **FOUND BY THE glm SEAT** -- a PACKET-FED transport, from the inlined function alone -- in
an answer I had recorded one sentence from and not re-read (regress/artifacts/sgirebufuninit/pass1_panel/ollama_glm.txt).  Verified here.

glm: *"`case 4' bounds `tile_nr' above only, so a negative `x' -- possible precisely because the sign check
is skipped for linear modes -- indexes `re_linear_a[-1]'."*

**THE THREE STEPS, EACH READ FROM THE SOURCE:**

    if (!linear && (x < 0 || y < 0 || x >= 2048 || y >= 2048))   <- SKIPPED when linear
            return;
    ...
    case 4: tile_nr = x >> 12;
            if (tile_nr >= 32)          <- bounds ABOVE only
                    return;
            tileptr = 0x80000000 | (d->re_linear_a[tile_nr] << 12);

    x = -1     -> tile_nr = -1   passes the >= 32 test  -> re_linear_a[-1]
    x = -8192  -> tile_nr = -2   passes                 -> re_linear_a[-2]

*** THE READ VALUE BECOMES A PHYSICAL ADDRESS, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS WORSE THAN A STRAY READ. ***
`tileptr = 0x80000000 | (d->re_linear_a[tile_nr] << 12)' -- so whatever struct field precedes `re_linear_a'
is shifted left 12 and used as the tile base, and the guest's pixel write then targets `tileptr + ofs'.  An
out-of-bounds READ of the device struct selects the DESTINATION of a subsequent write.

**THE REACHABILITY PATH IS COMPLETE AND GUEST-DRIVEN, and I traced it rather than assuming one exists:**
`step_x' is read from the guest register `CRIME_DE_XFER_STEP_X' into an `int32_t'; `src_x += step_x' runs in
the XFER loop; and the sanity check at `:734' *announces and CONTINUES* rather than declining -- grok
independently noted that same check is the file's only cross-field test and that it does not reconcile.  So a
guest writing a NEGATIVE step drives `src_x' negative into a linear-mode GET.

**NOT A DUPLICATE of [[sgilinearoob]]**, which is the ABOVE bound (`re_linear_[ab][tlbi+1]' with `tlbi'
capped at 31) in a different function.  This is the BELOW bound in `horrible_getputpixel''s case 4.  Same
array, opposite end, and the existing row's cap does not help here because the guard is a `>=' test that a
negative value passes.

**WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED:** which field precedes `re_linear_a' in the struct, and therefore what value the
OOB read actually yields -- that is layout-dependent and a round owes `offsetof' rather than a guess.  Also
unestablished is whether any real driver writes a negative step; the path is open, not observed.

*** THE SEAT NOTE WORTH KEEPING: A PACKET-FED SEAT FOUND THIS. ***  It cannot read the repo; it had the
function inlined and nothing else, and it noticed that one guard's precondition excludes the very mode the
other guard assumes.  The doctrine says packet-fed seats contribute attack REASONING rather than repo fact --
this is exactly that, and it is the strongest single finding any seat produced on this brief.

*** ESCALATED THE SAME HOUR: THE OUT-OF-BOUNDS READ LANDS ON GUEST-WRITABLE MEMORY, SO THE TILE POINTER
IS NOT MERELY STRAY -- IT IS CHOSEN.  Arithmetic and the write path both checked. ***

The declaration order is `re_tlb_a[256], re_tlb_b[256], re_tlb_c[256]` (uint16_t), then `re_tex[112]`
(uint16_t), then `re_linear_a[32]` (uint32_t):

    re_tlb_a..c   1536 bytes
    re_tex         224 bytes   -> ends at offset 1760
    1760 % 4 == 0              -> uint32_t needs no padding before it
    re_linear_a[-1] = bytes 1756..1759 = re_tex[110] and re_tex[111]

**And `re_tex` is written by the guest** -- `d->re_tex[tlbi] = data[hwi] * 256 + data[hwi+1];` in the
CRIME_RE_TEX store arm.

**THE COMPLETE CHAIN, each step read from the source rather than assumed:**

    1. guest stores to CRIME_RE_TEX, filling re_tex[110] and re_tex[111]
    2. guest sets CRIME_DE_XFER_STEP_X negative (int32_t; the :734 check ANNOUNCES and CONTINUES)
    3. src_x += step_x drives src_x negative in the XFER loop
    4. horrible_getputpixel with a LINEAR src_mode: the `x < 0' guard is skipped for linear
    5. case 4: tile_nr = x >> 12 = -1, and `if (tile_nr >= 32)' does not reject a negative
    6. tileptr = 0x80000000 | (re_linear_a[-1] << 12)   <- the two guest-written halfwords
    7. tileptr &= ~0x80000000; memory_rw(..., tileptr + ofs, buf, bufdepth, MEM_WRITE, PHYSICAL)

**So the guest selects the PHYSICAL DESTINATION of a device write.**  The value is shifted left 12, so the
reachable address space is large; `PHYSICAL' bypasses translation.

*** WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED, AND A ROUND OWES EACH BEFORE ANY CLAIM IS MADE OUTSIDE THIS FILE: ***
* **the layout arithmetic is a DERIVATION, not a measurement.**  It assumes no packing attribute and no
  compiler-inserted padding.  `offsetof' settles it in one line and MUST be run -- this project has a
  standing lesson that a struct-layout claim derived by hand was wrong, and the anchor rule's own exemplar
  turned on exactly this.
* **no witness.**  Every step is reachable by reading; none has been observed.
* **[[sgitexindex]] complicates step 1**: TEX writes OVERLAP (the index advances four per eight-byte
  register), so WHICH values land in `re_tex[110..111]' needs working out -- it affects controllability, not
  reachability.
* whether any real driver drives a negative step is unknown; the path is OPEN, not observed.

**RELATION TO THE OTHER ROWS:** [[sgilinearoob]] is the same array's ABOVE bound in a different function and
is unaffected.  [[sgirebufuninit]] shares the function but is about buffer CONTENTS; this is about the write
DESTINATION, and a memset fixes nothing here.  **The two must not be folded into one round** -- different
defect, different oracle, different severity.

*** THE `offsetof' THE ROW SAID MUST BE RUN HAS BEEN RUN.  ZERO PADDING -- THE ESCALATION HOLDS ON A
MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN ON MY ARITHMETIC. ***

    offsetof(re_tex)       = 1536
    re_tex ends at         = 1760
    offsetof(re_linear_a)  = 1760
    padding between        = 0 byte(s)

So `re_linear_a[-1]' is bytes 1756..1759 = `re_tex[110]' and `re_tex[111]', both written by the guest through
the CRIME_RE_TEX store arm.  Source preserved at `regress/artifacts/sgilinearnegidx/offcheck.c'.

*** AND THE FIRST ATTEMPT AT THIS MEASUREMENT PRODUCED A CONFIDENT WRONG ANSWER, BY A ROUTE THIS PROJECT HAS
NOT RECORDED BEFORE. ***  I wrote the test to `/tmp/off.c' from a Bash tool call and compiled it with
`wsl -- cc -o /tmp/off /tmp/off.c && /tmp/off'.  **git-bash's `/tmp' and WSL's `/tmp' are DIFFERENT
FILESYSTEMS.**  The heredoc wrote the Windows one; `cc' read WSL's, which held a stale `off.c' from an
earlier session; the compile SUCCEEDED, so `&&' could not catch it, and the program printed offsets for a
struct with `cmd' and `data' fields that appear nowhere in anything I wrote.

**The tell was the FIELD NAMES, not the exit status** -- the same shape as the carrier's stale-binary rule
(*a binary OLDER than its source*), reached by a different route: here the binary was fresh and the SOURCE
was the wrong file.  The existing rules do not cover it: no sentinel was owed, no tree was mutated, and every
status was 0.

**THE FIX IS THE ONE THE CARRIER ALREADY MANDATES FOR SCRIPTS, EXTENDED TO SOURCES: put the file on a
`/mnt/c' path both sides can see.**  The re-run also `rm's the binary first and refuses if none is produced,
so a stale artifact cannot answer for a failed build.

*** THE LINK I FLAGGED AS DOUBTFUL IS CONFIRMED, AND THE ANSWER IS SHARPER THAN THE CHAIN I WROTE:
ONE PREDICATE DISABLES ALL THREE PROTECTIONS.  Verified by direct reading 2026-09-07, after the
verification seat refused the brief. ***

I wrote that I was least sure of step 3 -- whether `src_x' is masked the way the destination `x' is, saying
that if it were, the chain dies there.  It is not, and the masking is CONDITIONAL on the very mode that
disables the other two guards:

    if (src_is_linear)
            src_x += step_x;                  <- NO MASK
    else
            src_x = (src_x + dx) & 0x7ff;     <- masked

**So `src_is_linear' simultaneously (a) removes the coordinate mask here, (b) skips the `x < 0' guard in
`horrible_getputpixel' via `if (!linear && (x < 0 ...))', and (c) routes to `case 4', whose `tile_nr' bound
is `>= 32' only.**  That is not three independent oversights lining up -- it is ONE predicate switching off
three protections at once, which is a much better description of the defect than my step list.

**THE REMAINING LINKS, each read at its own line:**

    :715   int32_t step_x = 0;                                  SIGNED
    :719   step_x = d->de_reg[CRIME_DE_XFER_STEP_X ...];        straight from a guest register
    :724   src_is_linear = ((src_mode & 0x00001c00) >> 10) > 3; guest-controlled via src_mode
    :757   uint16_t saved_src_x = src_x;                        so the row STARTS non-negative
    :912   if (src_is_linear) src_x += step_x;                  unmasked, per above

**MINIMAL REACHABILITY, which the earlier note did not state:** each row restarts at `saved_src_x' (a
`uint16_t', hence >= 0), the GET uses the CURRENT `src_x', and the increment happens after.  So with
`saved_src_x = 0' and `step_x = -1', **the SECOND pixel of the rectangle already uses `src_x = -1'** -- a
two-pixel-wide rectangle suffices.  No large geometry, no wraparound, no exotic value.

**STATUS: every link is now verified by reading.**  What remains unestablished is unchanged and stated
before: no witness has been run; [[sgitexindex]]'s overlapping TEX writes affect WHICH values land in
`re_tex[110..111]'; and no real driver is known to drive a negative step.

*** WITHDRAWN 2026-09-07.  THE FINDING IS FALSE.  `tile_nr' IS UNSIGNED, AND THE DECLARATION IS THREE
LINES ABOVE THE CODE I QUOTED. ***

    :204   int tile_nr_x = x / tilewidth_in_pixels;
    :205   int tile_nr_y = y >> 7;
    :207   unsigned int tile_nr = tile_nr_y * 16 + tile_nr_x;     <- UNSIGNED
    ...
    case 4: tile_nr = x >> 12;            <- converts to unsigned on assignment
            if (tile_nr >= 32) return;    <- 4294967295 >= 32 is TRUE.  IT RETURNS.

    x = -1     -> x >> 12 = -1  -> as unsigned = 4294967295  -> >= 32 -> REJECTED
    x = -8192  -> x >> 12 = -2  -> as unsigned = 4294967294  -> >= 32 -> REJECTED

**The guard I called `upper bound only' is a COMPLETE bound**, because the conversion folds every negative
value into the rejected range.  There is no out-of-bounds read, no guest-chosen tile pointer, and no write
primitive.  Refuted by the codex seat (regress/artifacts/sgilinearnegidx/codex_siblings_20260907.txt).

*** HOW BADLY I GOT THIS WRONG, RECORDED IN FULL BECAUSE THE PROCESS FAILURE IS THE ONLY THING OF VALUE
LEFT IN THIS ROW. ***

* I filed it HIGH, then ESCALATED it to a guest-chosen physical write address.
* I wrote *"every link is now verified by reading"* -- and had verified the link I DOUBTED (whether `src_x'
  is masked) while never checking the TYPE of the index variable, which is the most basic property of an
  index and the one that decides the whole question.
* I ran an `offsetof' to avoid trusting hand arithmetic on the struct layout.  **That measurement is
  correct and it was aimed at the wrong link.**  Rigour on one step does not transfer to the step you did
  not question.
* **THE DECLARATION WAS ON MY SCREEN.**  I printed lines 184-215 of this function earlier in the same
  session while checking the mode decode; `unsigned int tile_nr' is at 207, inside that range.  I read past
  it because I was looking for the mode fields.
* It is in commit `15633bb`'s MESSAGE as a headline claim, which cannot be edited.  **That message is
  wrong** and this row is the correction a reader must reach.

**WHAT SURVIVES:** the `offsetof' result (`re_tex` ends at 1760, `re_linear_a` begins at 1760, zero
padding) is a true measurement, preserved at `regress/artifacts/sgilinearnegidx/offcheck.c'.  It is about a
path nothing can reach, so it supports no finding.

*** AND THE REFUSAL COST ME THE REFUTATION FOR HOURS, WHICH IS THE SHARPEST ARGUMENT YET ABOUT §C5. ***  I
asked the seat to attack this chain link by link.  **That brief was REFUSED for being chain-shaped.**  The
same seat, asked the same subject WITHOUT the chain -- *which array indexes are bounded on one side only?*
-- answered in one line: *"the stated case-4 underflow is absent in this fork: `tile_nr' is unsigned."*
**The refusal did not stop a bad question; it delayed a correct answer**, and in the interval I escalated a
false finding, wrote it into a commit, and reported it as the session's most severe result.

*The lesson is not that seats are unreliable.  I built this chain, I verified the parts I doubted, and I
was wrong about the part I never questioned.  The seat that could have caught it earlier was refused for
the SHAPE of my question rather than its content.*

**WHAT THE SAME AUDIT DID FIND, and it is not this row's defect:** *"There are missing checks on complete
write SPANS in TLB_A/B/C and LINEAR_A/B, whose safety depends on caller alignment."*  A span check is a
different question from an index bound -- the index can be in range while the multi-byte write starting
there runs past the end.  **Filed separately as [[sgirespanchk]] rather than folded in here**, because a
withdrawn row is the worst possible place to hide a live one.

rows.title: dev_sgi_re.c: the TLB_A/B/C and LINEAR_A/B write loops bound only the FIRST element of a multi-element span -- a handler ROBUSTNESS gap, with the alignment that makes it unreachable VERIFIED in the CPU load/store path rather than assumed
rows.witness: none
rows.state_note:
FILED 2026-09-07, SPLIT OUT OF THE WITHDRAWN [[sgilinearnegidx]] ROW.

**Kept separate on purpose: a withdrawn entry is the worst possible place to hide a live finding.**  The
same codex audit that REFUTED the negative-index claim (`tile_nr` is unsigned, so the `>= 32` guard rejects
every negative x) continued in its verdict line:

    "There are missing checks on complete write SPANS in TLB_A/B/C and LINEAR_A/B, whose safety
     depends on caller alignment."

**A SPAN CHECK IS A DIFFERENT QUESTION FROM AN INDEX BOUND.**  A bound of the form `if (i >= n) return;`
answers *where does the access START*; it says nothing about where a multi-element access FINISHES.  An
index can be in range while the span running from it leaves the array.  So the refutation of the
negative-index chain does not touch this at all -- they are independent claims about the same arrays.

*** STATUS: AN AUDIT VERDICT, NOT A VERIFIED FINDING, AND THE DISTINCTION IS THE WHOLE POINT OF FILING IT
THIS WAY. ***  The verdict CONDITIONS the safety on caller alignment rather than asserting a defect -- the
seat's own words are *"whose safety depends on"*, which is a statement about an unchecked assumption, not
about a reachable bug.  **An unchecked assumption that happens to hold is a different thing from a checked
one**, and this row must not be promoted until somebody says which of the two it is.

**OWED, and the third is the load-bearing one:**
  1. the arrays with their declared element counts, and every multi-element access site;
  2. where each span's WIDTH comes from -- a constant, or a register-derived value;
  3. **whether any CALLER can present an unaligned or oversized span.**  If every caller is bounded by
     construction this is a robustness note; if one is not, it is a defect.

A read-only audit is out (`regress/artifacts/sgirespanchk/SPAN_brief.md`, fired at the codex seat 2026-09-07
under the C5 scoping rules -- reading scoped to `src/`, no chain, no reachability question).  **The brief
opens by telling the seat that my last brief stated a false premise about an index variable's TYPE and asks
it to read the declarations**, which is the premise-audit instruction aimed at the exact error that produced
this row's parent.

*Provenance worth keeping: this finding was in the SAME verdict line as the refutation, and I nearly lost it
-- the refutation was the arresting half and the span sentence sat after it.  That is the under-harvest
shape this session has already hit five times: take the finding, skip the rest of the sentence.*

*** UPDATED WITHIN THE HOUR, AND IT IS A DOWNGRADE: THE SAME ANSWER ALREADY CONTAINED THE
CALLER-ALIGNMENT CHECK I HAD JUST FIRED A SECOND BRIEF TO OBTAIN.  MED -> LOW. ***

**I filed this row from the verdict LINE and had not yet read the body.**  The body enumerates the spans and
then answers the question the verdict left open:

    | Each TLB write loop    | 253 | 253, 254, 255, **256**      |
    | Each TLB write loop    | 254 | 254, 255, **256, 257**      |
    | Each TLB write loop    | 255 | 255, **256, 257, 258**      |
    | Each LINEAR write pair |  31 | 31, **32**                  |

    "These are HANDLER ROBUSTNESS GAPS, not established guest out-of-bounds writes.  For the normal
     SGI CPU access paths checked, eight-byte accesses have eight-byte alignment.  Enumerating aligned
     addresses gives TLB starting indexes 0,4,...,252, and LINEAR starting indexes 0,2,...,30; their
     complete spans fit.  I VERIFIED THE ALIGNMENT HANDLING IN THE ORDINARY ACCESS CODE AND
     UNALIGNED-ACCESS HELPER, RATHER THAN ACCEPTING THE DEVICE COMMENTS."

-- `src/cpus/cpu_mips_instr_loadstore.c` and `src/cpus/cpu_mips_instr_unaligned.c`, both named.

**THAT IS THE DIFFERENCE THIS ROW WAS FILED TO DEMAND, AND IT WAS ALREADY DISCHARGED.**  The row asked
whether the safety is a CHECKED property or an unchecked assumption that happens to hold.  The seat checked
it, in the right files, and said so in the words that distinguish the two.  So: a robustness gap in the
device handler, unreachable through the CPU paths that exist.

**WHAT IS STILL OPEN, and it is narrow: the word "checked".**  The seat verified the MIPS load/store and
unaligned paths.  It did NOT enumerate every route into `dev_sgi_re`'s access function -- a DMA engine, a
device-to-device access, or the debugger's `put` reach a handler without going through a CPU load.  A
second read-only audit is already running (`SPAN_brief.md`) whose Q4 asks exactly this, and it was written
and fired BEFORE this body was read, so its answer is independent rather than a re-confirmation.

*** THIS IS THE FIFTH UNDER-HARVEST OF THE SESSION AND THE FIRST WHERE IT COST A WHOLE INVOCATION. ***  The
previous four dropped a seat's REFUTATION while keeping its finding.  This one dropped the seat's own
DISCHARGE of the obligation I then wrote into a row and spent a codex run re-asking.  **The verdict line is
a summary written against the brief's framing and is the LEAST likely part of an answer to carry the
qualification** -- this file already says so about corrections, and it is equally true of discharges.

*Also harvested from the same body, each a check I had not asked for: `de_reg[1024]` accessed at `[regnr]`
and `[regnr+1]` reaches at most 512 (safe); the two static `rop_used[256]` arrays are masked `& 255`, which
supplies BOTH bounds; `zerobuf[4096]` is length-capped then page-shortened, never enlarged; and `buf[8]`
takes enumerated lengths 1/2/4/8 which fit -- with the seat noting unprompted that its INITIALISATION is a
separate defect, which is [[sgirebufuninit]], already filed.*

**AND ONE FINDING THAT IS NEW AND IS NOT A SPAN QUESTION:** *"the coordinate rectangle check does not by
itself establish the TLB capacity bound."*  At depth field 3 (`bufdepth` 8, tile width 64) the pre-guard
`tile_nr` reaches **271**, not 255 -- the `x,y < 2048` rectangle admits indexes past the end of a `[256]`
array, and it is the LATER `tile_nr >= 256` guard that rejects them.  Both bounds are present so nothing is
broken; what is worth recording is that **the two guards are not redundant, and an edit removing the second
one as "already covered by the rectangle check" would open a 16-element overrun.**  That is a clause-(d)
shaped hazard sitting in code nobody is currently editing -- noted here, not filed.
