S5 ALSO NEEDED QUALIFYING: the attach is unconditional WITHIN THE MVME187 BRANCH.  MVME188 and MVME197 do not attach the device.

*** THE VERDICT IS A ONE-TOKEN BOUNDARY CORRECTION, member 6 (BACKED ACCEPT). ***  In the accept block, replace `relative_addr < MK48T08_CLKOFF' with `relative_addr < MK48T08_CLKOFF + MK48TXX_ICSR', keeping the upper comparison at MK48TXX_ISEC.  Enumerated: the switch then sees EXACTLY 0x1ff8, which is the only case it has, **the default arm becomes UNREACHABLE**, and the eight NVRAM bytes go to the RAM path where d->reg[] already has storage.  Neither vendored constant is wrong -- the lower comparison was simply missing its `+ MK48TXX_ICSR'.

*** A FLOOR PROBLEM THE ROUND MUST STATE RATHER THAN FUDGE, and the seat raised it unprompted: THE SMALLEST EDIT REMOVES NO KILL STATEMENT. ***  It makes the existing default unreachable.  So a clause-(b) 'verbatim reinstatement of the removed defect' is either a no-op or unreachable code, and NO behavioural channel can distinguish it -- the floor cannot be satisfied literally for that mutant.  The distinguishable mutant is RESTORING THE OLD DISPATCH, i.e. the old boundary plus its fatal, and it must be named separately.

*** AND A ROUTING TRAP THAT WOULD MAKE A PROBE VACUOUS: this device registers DM_DEFAULT, so memory_rw.c SKIPS its callback for NO_EXCEPTIONS accesses (DM_READS_HAVE_NO_SIDE_EFFECTS is absent).  Success and zero-filled reads through that route would not demonstrate the repaired device behaviour at all. ***  A debugger-`dump'-based oracle is therefore worthless here; the probe must use real guest loads.  This is the carrier's own SH4 `dump' finding recurring on a different device.

CLOCK-WRITE SEMANTICS TRACED, which settles whether d->reg[] is a safe backing store: guest time writes are stored immediately without consulting CSR_WRITE, read back as stored, and overwritten from host UTC on the next RISING edge of the READ bit.  **The eight newly admitted NVRAM slots are separate array elements the updater neither reads nor writes**, so accepting those writes cannot contaminate a later clock value.  Separate fidelity gaps exist (unlatched reads do not advance; the WRITE-bit commit protocol is absent) and are NOT this round's.

TEN DETECTOR ROWS PRESCRIBED with a named mutant and a differing observable each, including a NULLED-REPAIR family (guard corrected, backing assignment removed) and the caution that **correct storage and dropped storage are both SILENT**, so no row may claim that kill through a diagnostic count.  No in-tree consumer depends on termination at these eight offsets; the MVME PROM emulation contains no clock/NVRAM access at all.

*** WITNESSED AND FIXED 2026-09-10 -- the round is IN WORK, fix in the tree, detector and pass 2 still owed. ***

THE WITNESS (Opus measuring seat, rung 3): 15/47 on the committed build, 46/47 after the fix.  The oracle is a CONJUNCTION of the reaped wait status and a POST-ACCESS OBSERVABLE -- a scratch store before the access under test and a scratch load after it -- so a death, a hang and a fatal() that merely complains are three DISTINGUISHABLE states.  That matters here: this fork's fatal() has no early-out and does NOT exit, so 'it printed a message' is not evidence of death, and a timeout gets its own token rather than being read as a kill.

*** TWO MEASURED CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN FILING, both from the seat. ***
  (1) THE POPULATION IS SIXTEEN CELLS, NOT EIGHT: every one of the eight offsets kills in BOTH directions, ld.bu and st.b alike, and all sixteen were driven.  A round that drove reads only would have left half its own defect unwitnessed.
  (2) THE KILL IS WIDTH-INDEPENDENT: `len' never enters the guard, so ld / ld.h / ld.bu all die at the same start offset.  **There is therefore NO width axis to close**, and a detector row varying width at a fixed offset would be non-varying by construction -- the CHANNEL vacuity this project names.  This is the opposite of dev_pcc2.c, where width WAS the defect.

AND THE SEAT REACHED THE REGISTER-BANK FINDING INDEPENDENTLY of the codex design seat, from the other direction: nvramsz - 16 = 8192 - 16 = 0x1ff0 is exactly the vendored header's 'first bank of eight registers ... available only on more recent models'.  Two seats, two routes, same conclusion -- which is worth more than either alone, because neither was told the other's answer.

*** THE PROBE CANNOT SCORE 47/47 ON ANY BUILD, BY CONSTRUCTION, and this must not be read as a residual failure. ***  Its `msg census' row asserts that all sixteen deaths named their own offset in the diagnostic text -- a DEFECT-SIGNATURE row, green only while the defect is present.  Post-fix there are no deaths, so it correctly reads 0 of 16.  The 32 kill rows and that one row are mutually exclusive.  **A shipped detector must DROP or INVERT it**; carried as-is it can never be green, which is a different fault from the one it was written to catch.

THE BOUNDARY MOVE DID NOT SWALLOW THE LEGITIMATE CASE -- the design's own question 3 -- and it is measured, not argued: `ok rd 1ff8' and `ok wr 1ff8' are green on both builds, so 0x1ff8 still reaches the switch and its ICSR case still does its work.

A SECOND, NON-FATAL DEFECT IN THE SAME HANDLER, raised by the seat and OUT OF SCOPE here: the accept path reads and writes exactly ONE byte whatever `len' says, so a 4-byte read of the clock block returns 0x00000005 where a true big-endian device read would give 0x05100926.  Measured.  It is a wrong-value defect rather than a kill, it sits three lines above this one, and routing the eight NVRAM offsets to that same path gives them the same behaviour -- which should be a DECISION rather than an accident.  Filed separately rather than folded in.

*** AND THE SEAT FOUND A DEFECT IN ITS OWN PROBE AND REPORTED IT RATHER THAN QUIETLY FIXING IT. *** Its first run scored 13/46 with a devsig control red; the WANT was wrong and the device was right -- C's struct tm has tm_mon 0-based while Python's is 1-based.  Had that been a KILL row instead of a control it would have shipped a false positive.  That is the 'did it fail for the reason under test?' guard doing its job.
rows.witness: probe:regress/artifacts/mk48nvramkill/opus_mk48_nvram_witness_20260910.py -- RUNG 3 on unmodified `-E mvme88k -e mvme187', real MC88100 instructions through real decode and real memory_rw, nothing added to reach the site.  MEASURED BEFORE THE EDIT: 15/47 (opus_witness_run_20260910.txt), all 15 controls green and all 32 kill rows red.  AFTER: 46/47 (postfix_run_20260910.txt), every kill row green and every control held.  SHIPPED DETECTOR: regress/mk48_nvram_probe.py, 57 rows, killtable_20260910/t3/SCORES.txt -- BASE 57/57, null medium 16/57, five mutants 16..56/57, ZERO ESCAPES, restore verified on both parts.

closure.note: FIXED AND SHIPPED AS #521.  Eight ordinary NVRAM bytes inside the device's own 8192-byte registration fell to a default: arm that calls exit(1); the accept block's lower bound was one term short.  ONE TOKEN fixes it, and it is a BOUNDARY CORRECTION rather than new policy because the backing storage already existed.  Witnessed at rung 3 BEFORE the edit (15/47 -> 46/47) with a conjunction oracle -- wait status AND a post-access observable -- so death, a hang and a fatal() that merely prints are three distinguishable states, which matters because this fork's fatal() does not exit.  TWO measured corrections to the filing: the population is SIXTEEN cells not eight, and the kill is WIDTH-INDEPENDENT so there is no width axis to close.  THE DETECTOR TOOK TWO REPAIRS, both of the SAME CLASS: table 1 found the survive-only hole at the control register (M_ICSR escaped 47/47 because the mutated condition is a tautology and the rows there assert only that the access completed), and pass 2 found it again on the eight accepted bytes.  Two consecutive findings triggered the class closure -- nine round-trip rows in one diff, each writing a distinct byte.  AND PASS 2 CAUGHT AN APPARATUS DEFECT IN THE ROUND'S OWN TABLE: M_NULL replaced a statement with a COMMENT, which is whitespace, so `goto ret' became the if-body and the leg measured a different mutant while the record claimed clause (d) was satisfied; rebuilt braced, and t3 measures exactly what was claimed.  Floor clause (b) is unsatisfiable literally -- this diff removes no kill, it makes one unreachable -- and the round says so and substitutes M_OLD rather than pretending.  SEATS: the fix ratified by every seat expressing a view; fable5 WALLED with no substitute, re-fired once, named; kimi CLI walled and COVERED by its cloud substitute; agy deliberately not fired.  One BREACH verdict REFUTED with its warrant (the rows it said were missing exist).

rows.title: cpu_mips_instr.c EXT / DEXTM / DEXTU: the extraction shift count goes NEGATIVE for 496 of 1024 field pairs per opcode, driven straight from a guest instruction word -- and PLAIN DEXT is CLEAN, so the bad pairs reach the shared handler through the two variants' field adjustments rather than through dext itself
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10.  Surfaced by the GPT-6 Astra fix-design review on [[armbfiwidth]], which went looking for siblings of that round's idiom and found this outside ARM.  RE-DERIVED LOCALLY before filing.

X(ext) computes `int size = msbd + 1;` then `x = (rs << (32-lsb-size)) >> (32-lsb-size);` with msbd and lsb each decoded independently from the instruction word in 0..31. **Enumerating all 1024 pairs: 496 give a NEGATIVE shift count.**  `rs` is uint32_t so the left operand is unsigned and form (c) does not arise -- but a NEGATIVE COUNT is undefined regardless of the operand's type, which is the trap: a reader checking `is this unsigned?' passes this site.

X(dext) is the same shape at 64 bits and is WORSE in a way that looks like a fix: the count is CAST, `(rs << (uint64_t)(64-lsb-size))`.  **The cast does not rescue it.**  A negative int converted to uint64_t becomes an enormous positive value, so the count is then >= the width of the type -- form (b) instead of form (a), still undefined.  A cast that converts one undefined form into another while reading as a precaution is worth recording as a pattern.

*** WHY THIS IS A FIELD-VALIDATION DEFECT AND NOT A CAST DEFECT, which decides the fix. *** The MIPS architecture REQUIRES lsb + size <= 32 for EXT (and the corresponding bound for the dext family); an encoding violating it is architecturally invalid.  So the right repair is probably to DECLINE or to raise the architectural exception for the invalid encodings, not to paper the shift over with a cast -- a mask repair would give a defined answer to a question the guest was not entitled to ask, and would silently make invalid encodings look supported.  That is a design question for a panel, not a one-line edit, which is why this is filed MED/not-easy while the [[shiftubcensus]] members are filed as one-token repairs.

REACHABILITY: MIPS is this project's primary architecture with the most exercised rigs, and the count comes straight from the instruction word with no CPU-model gate, so a guest need only execute one malformed EXT.  NOT measured, and no witness built -- what is established is the domain arithmetic and the decode, both re-derived here.

SCOPE NOTE: distinct from [[shiftubcensus]], which is the SIGNED-1 family (`1 << n` where the literal is a plain int).  This is the NEGATIVE-COUNT family, a different C99 clause and a different fix shape.  A tree-wide census separating the three forms was fired at the codex seat on 2026-09-10 and its answer belongs to shiftubcensus.

*** DESIGN REVIEW 2026-09-10 (mipsextshift/codex_design_20260910.txt, GPT-6 Astra at max, ZERO TERMINAL cyber flags -- one MID-STREAM flag, retried, non-fatal, which is the position discriminator working as designed).  VERDICT: **FAULT**, and it CORRECTED THIS ROW IN FOUR PLACES. ***

**(1) PLAIN DEXT HAS NO BAD FIELD PAIRS AT ALL.  MY TITLE WAS WRONG.**  Enumerated per opcode, all 1024 raw pairs including packing and unpacking:
        EXT     msbd 0-31   lsb 0-31   middle count -31..31   **496 negative**
        DEXT    msbd 0-31   lsb 0-31   middle count   1..63   **ZERO negative**
        DEXTM   msbd 32-63  lsb 0-31   middle count -31..31   **496 negative**
        DEXTU   msbd 0-31   lsb 32-63  middle count -31..31   **496 negative**
  DEXTM adds 32 to msbd and DEXTU adds 32 to lsb, BEFORE packing the arguments for the shared handler.  **So X(dext) is a victim rather than a culprit: it is fed out-of-range fields by the two variants.**  The title is corrected; a fix aimed at `dext' would have been aimed at the wrong place.

**(2) THERE ARE ADMISSION GATES, contrary to this row's broader claim.**  SPECIAL3 rejects older ISA/revision combinations, R5900 takes another path, and `rt == $zero' selects a NOP.  So the field domains are unconstrained WHEN THE HANDLER ACTUALLY RUNS, but not every MIPS model or destination reaches it.  My row implied no gating at all.

**(3) RI IS PERMITTED, NOT MANDATED -- and this is exactly the overclaim the row warned itself about.**  The local manuals say EXT's excessive field sum is UNPREDICTABLE, and that ordinary DEXT has no UNPREDICTABLE field case while DEXTM/U do.  The manual's own definition of UNPREDICTABLE PERMITS arbitrary exceptions while FORBIDDING processor halt or hang.  So declining is a sound emulator policy and claiming the architecture requires a Reserved Instruction exception would overstate it.

**(4) THE DINS-FAMILY EXECUTION HANDLERS DO NOT EXIST IN THIS TREE**, so the sibling question I asked about ins/dins/dinsm/dinsu is partly moot.

THE PRESCRIBED FIX IS TWO DECODER GUARDS, not a mask and not a cast: reject `lsb + msbd + 1 > 32' for EXT and `> 64' for the shared DEXT/DEXTM/DEXTU case AFTER the variant adjustments, setting `ic->f = instr(reserved)' and breaking **BEFORE the $zero NOP shortcut** -- the ordering matters, because a NOP shortcut taken first would swallow the rejection.  *That places the bound where the fields are normalised, which is the only place one bound can serve all three variants.*

*** DESIGNED 2026-09-10 (mipsextshift/codex_guards_RETRY_20260910.txt, GPT-6 Astra at max, ZERO cyber flags).  THE DESIGN IS COMPLETE AND TWO OF MY PREMISES WERE WRONG. ***

**REFUTED (1): I gave plain DEXT the constraint `0 < pos + size <= 32'.  The specification says `<= 63'** (mips64_volII.txt:550) -- plain DEXT can extract a field CROSSING BIT 31 and is not confined to the low word.  My CONCLUSION survives (DEXT is safe) and my REASON did not, which is the direction that matters: the safety comes from `64 - b - (m+1) = 63 - (b+m)' with `0 <= b+m <= 62', giving a count of 1..63.  *The row's title has now been wrong once in each direction on this same instruction.*

**REFUTED (2): I wrote that a negative count is `in practice reduced modulo the width'.  C99 guarantees no such thing**, and the two handlers do not even fail the same way: in `X(ext)' the negative `int' is the shift count directly, while in `X(dext)' it is CONVERTED TO `uint64_t' first, producing an enormous unsigned count that still exceeds the operand width.  Two routes to undefined behaviour, one of which my description did not contain.

**CONFIRMED, with a better derivation than mine: 496 per affected opcode, and all three reduce to the SAME expression** -- EXT `32-b-(m+1)', DEXTM `64-b-(m+33)', DEXTU `64-(b+32)-(m+1)' are each exactly `31 - (b+m)', negative precisely when `b+m >= 32'.  For each `m' the invalid `b' run is `32-m .. 31', i.e. `m' values, and `sum(0..31) = 496'.  Enumerated exhaustively as well as derived.  **The field ADJUSTMENTS are correct**: the spec's own encoded fields are `msbdminus32' and `lsbminus32', so `msbd += 32' and `lsb += 32' are what it asks for.

**DISPOSITION: member 5, FAULT -- `ic->f = instr(reserved);' -- on the file's own precedent** (the ISA-support check immediately above this switch uses exactly that), and it is available here because `X(reserved)' syncs the pc and calls `mips_cpu_exception(cpu, EXCEPTION_RI, ...)', which does NOT call exit() and does not end the host.  The specification permits it: *`UNPREDICTABLE operations may cause arbitrary exceptions'* (mips64_volII.txt:44).  The three affected pages say UNPREDICTABLE (`:746', `:562', `:570'); plain DEXT's page says outright *`there is no UNPREDICTABLE case for this instruction'* (`:554').

THE GUARDS, and the placement is confirmed load-bearing:

    EXT block:                  if (lsb + msbd + 1 > 32) { ic->f = instr(reserved); break; }
    DEXT/DEXTM/DEXTU block:     if (lsb + msbd + 1 > 64) { ic->f = instr(reserved); break; }
                                -- AFTER the two `+= 32' adjustments

No lower bound is owed (the field widths supply it), and equality with the width is LEGAL and yields a zero shift count.  The inner `break' leaves `switch (s6)' and so also defeats the `rt == MIPS_GPR_ZERO' no-op rewrite -- **deliberate**: an invalid pair targeting register zero still takes RI.

*** THE ORDERING MUTANT IS THE STRONGEST ONE AND IT IS BETTER THAN I GUESSED: the shared predicate placed BEFORE the adjustments REJECTS NOTHING AT ALL. ***  Its left-hand side is then at most 31+31+1 = 63, which is never `> 64', so all 496 DEXTM and all 496 DEXTU invalid pairs sail through -- a guard that reads correctly, compiles, and is identically inert.  Two more: `+ 1' -> `+ 0' is one character, stays valid C, and admits the first forbidden endpoint (31 pairs per opcode); `>' -> `>=' fails in the OTHER direction, wrongly rejecting the legal equality cases.  A detector must distinguish those two.

**ROUND SCOPE: TWO changes, not three.**  DEXTM and DEXTU share one decoder site, one normalisation, one predicate and one handler, and DEXT rides in the same block; EXT is the second site.  Both meet same-file and same-class -- **but the same-detector condition is NOT demonstrated**, so the default stands at two.  One combined round qualifies only if a single parameterised decoder-SELECTION test covers all four opcodes, whose common oracle is `does every requested source-bit position lie within the source width' plus the expected handler choice.

*** NO RUNNABLE REPRODUCTION IS ESTABLISHED, AND THAT IS THE ROUND'S REAL BLOCKER. ***  EXT is **MIPS32 Release 2** (`:746') and the doubleword forms are **MIPS64 Release 2** (`:550', `:558', `:566') -- so they are NOT available merely because this tree boots a MIPS machine, and no machine has been named that runs them.  The rung-3 attempt is owed before this may be recorded documented-only.

**AND THE SEAT DECLINED THE ONE THING I ASKED FOR THAT I SHOULD NOT HAVE**, on grounds worth keeping: I asked for the wrong VALUE a bad pair produces, and there is no sound portable oracle for it -- the architecture declares the case UNPREDICTABLE and the C is undefined, so no particular value is a legitimate expectation.  It supplied DECODER-SELECTION assertions instead (invalid fields select `reserved' before any extraction runs; valid fields keep their handler or `nop'; the permitted endpoint stays accepted; 496 rejections per affected opcode and zero for DEXT).  *That is the substitute form added to BRIEF_TEMPLATE.md §C5 the same hour, validated on its first use.*

SCOPE CAVEAT THE SEAT STATED ITSELF: it found no other constructor of these handlers and no direct caller **in this file**, but `cpu_mips_instr.c' is `#include'd into a larger compilation and the other members were outside its permitted paths.  So the no-handler-check conclusion is file-scoped, not repository-wide.

NEW FINDING, FILED SEPARATELY as [[mipsextsignext]]: **EXT carries a SECOND restriction these guards do not address** -- it requires a properly sign-extended 32-bit source value (`:746', reflected in its operation at `:750').  Nothing in the handler or the decoder checks it.

rows.title: dev_dreamcast_maple.c MAPLE_DMAADDR read: the handler assigns the CORRECT value to odata and then calls exit(1), so an ordinary guest read of a register the model fully implements ends the emulator -- option-set member 4 (ACCEPT), two lines deleted
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10 from the GPT-6 Astra exit audit (regress/artifacts/queuetriage/codex_exitaudit_20260910.txt), which ranked it I1/E1. VERIFIED LOCALLY by opening the file before filing.

The read arm of `case 0x04: /* MAPLE_DMAADDR */` reads, in order:
    fatal("[ dreamcast_maple: TODO: read from dmaaddr ]\n");
    odata = d->dmaaddr;
    exit(1);
**The correct value is computed and then thrown away by terminating the process.**  The WRITE arm two lines above stores `d->dmaaddr = idata', so the register is FULLY MODELLED in both directions -- a guest that writes the DMA address and reads it back, which is the ordinary way to confirm a controller programming step, is killed on the read.

REACHABILITY: machine_dreamcast.c adds `dreamcast_maple' unconditionally.  Nothing has to start DMA or build a command list; the plain readback reaches it.

*** THIS IS THE ACCEPT MEMBER'S TEXTBOOK SHAPE, which the option set records as member 4: the model ALREADY computes the right value and then discards it, so the disposition is to delete the kill and KEEP THE VALUE, with NO latch -- there is no event to announce, and a bounded announce would ship a wrong record in product code (an `unimplemented; ignored' message about a read that is implemented and is not ignored). ***  Two deleted lines.

FAULT is not available and would be wrong anyway: memory_rw.c converts a failed device callback into an architectural access exception for MIPS and M88K ONLY, and this device sits on an SH4 machine -- but the access is implemented, so refusing it would be the wrong answer even if the machinery existed.

TEST CARRIER EXISTS: regress/gdrom_default_probe.py already supplies a Dreamcast session with guest load/store helpers.  The oracle must assert that a separately STORED value reads back EXACTLY and that execution continues -- observing a zero, or a surviving debugger prompt, would be a vacuous row, since both are true of several wrong implementations.

NOT MEASURED and no witness built.  The rung-3 attempt is owed before this may be recorded documented-only.

*** DESIGN REVIEW 2026-09-10 (acceptclass/codex_acceptclass_20260910.txt): VERDICT IS **HOLD** THE TWO-LINE ACCEPT, AND IT REFUTED A PREMISE OF MINE.  Both points verified locally before recording. ***

**MY PREMISE 'the correct value is computed and then thrown away' IS TOO GENEROUS.**  `odata` is a LOCAL.  The copy that delivers it -- `memory_writemax64(cpu, data, len, odata)' -- sits at the FUNCTION TAIL, after the switch, so `exit(1)' fires first and **the value never reaches the caller at all**.  The fix is unchanged (deleting the kill lets execution reach the tail and the value IS then delivered), but the DESCRIPTION was wrong and a wrong description gets reused.

**AND THE ROUND IS HELD ON A SEMANTIC QUESTION I DID NOT ASK: what should a read of the DMA address RETURN?**  Real Maple hardware may advance a DMA cursor, in which case a post-transfer readback should give the ADVANCED cursor rather than the address the guest programmed.  The model stores only what was written.  So ACCEPT-as-stored may be shipping a plausible wrong value in place of a loud stop, which is the worse outcome and is exactly the hazard the brief's own question 2 raised about the `TODO'.  **The round owes a settled hardware contract before it may ship**, and the detector's `A.afterdma' row must take its expected value FROM THAT CONTRACT rather than from today's implementation -- with transfer evidence alongside the address readback, so that skipping DMA cannot manufacture a pass.

*** THE HELD QUESTION WAS AIMED AT THE WRONG ARM, AND THE TREE ANSWERS IT ITSELF.  Found 2026-09-10 by opening the file, in under two minutes, which is what the check-do-not-judge rule is for. ***

The review held this round on *what should a read of the DMA address RETURN -- the programmed address, or an ADVANCED cursor?*, and warned that ACCEPT-as-stored might ship a plausible wrong value in place of a loud stop.  **The premise under that question is that the model stores only what was written.  IT DOES NOT.**

`maple_do_dma_xfer()' walks the command list accumulating `addr += datalen_cmd * 4' and then, at its tail, immediately before asserting SYSASIC_EVENT_MAPLE_DMADONE:

        // TODO: Should the DMA address be updated?
        d->dmaaddr = addr;

**So the advancing cursor is ALREADY MODELLED, and the tree flags its own uncertainty about it in a comment one line above.**  A read after a transfer would return the ADVANCED address; a read before any transfer returns the programmed one.

*** WHAT THAT CHANGES: THE TWO QUESTIONS ARE ON DIFFERENT SITES AND ONLY ONE OF THEM IS THIS ROUND'S. ***  The read arm does not decide what `d->dmaaddr' holds -- it is a pure reporter of a field that `maple_do_dma_xfer()' owns.  Whether the advance is architecturally right is a PRE-EXISTING open question at a DIFFERENT site, which this round neither creates nor resolves, and deleting the read-side termination leaves it exactly where it was.  **Filed separately as [[mapledmaadvance]] rather than folded in here** -- the same discipline the sibling review applied to [[xscaleinten]], where a write-side kill on the adjacent case was ruled a separate row.

**AND THE `plausible wrong value versus a loud stop' TRADE IS WEAKER THAN IT LOOKS, in two ways worth stating rather than glossing.**  The loud stop is `exit(1)' -- it ends the emulator, so nobody acts on it as a diagnostic; and the SAME unverified address is ALREADY handed to the DMA engine on every transfer, so the exposure the review is protecting against exists whether or not a guest ever reads the register back.  The read arm is the one place the value is currently NOT consumed.

**THE DETECTOR CONSEQUENCE, which is the part the review was right to press on:** the after-DMA row must NOT pin the advanced value as architecturally correct, because this round has not established that.  It pins the READ ARM'S contract, which is what the diff changes -- (i) a stored value reads back exactly with no transfer in between, and (ii) the value read after a transfer DIFFERS from the programmed one, which proves the read reports the live field rather than a constant or a stale snapshot -- with transfer evidence alongside, so that a skipped DMA cannot manufacture a pass.  The advanced value's CORRECTNESS is [[mapledmaadvance]]'s to pin, and the contract paragraph says so under clause (e).

*Recorded before any seat was asked, then sent for checking rather than acted on: the review that raised the hold was right that the round owed an answer, and the answer turned out to be in the file rather than in a datasheet.*

*** REVIEWED 2026-09-10 (mapledmaaddr/codex_readarm_20260910.txt, GPT-6 Astra at max, ZERO cyber flags).  VERDICT: **THE READ-ARM CORRECTION MAY PROCEED INDEPENDENTLY.**  My state trace was right, my observability claim was wrong, and MY PROPOSED DETECTOR IS INSUFFICIENT. ***

**THE SEPARATION HOLDS**, on a bounded basis the review stated rather than assumed: the read correction implements a separately testable rule -- *return the stored register field* -- while the cursor item decides what the transfer routine should STORE there.  The cursor policy already affects execution beyond this arm, since a subsequent transfer starts from `d->dmaaddr' and so already consumes the advanced value whether or not any guest reads it.

**BUT MY FRAMING WAS TOO STRONG IN ONE PLACE, and the correction is exact:** *"the edit does not change cursor computation"* is correct; *"the edit does not change the OBSERVABILITY of that computation"* would NOT be -- a guest read that previously stopped execution can now obtain the field.  That is a new observable, and the round must say so rather than claim the diff is behaviour-preserving.

THREE CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN NOTE ABOVE, all from reading the file:
  1. **The advance is MORE than the payload increment I quoted.**  Each descriptor advances by **8 bytes of control words + 4 bytes of command word + 4*datalen_cmd of data**, so the committed value is `C = (P + SUM(12 + 4*D_i)) mod 2^32'.  I wrote only the `4 * datalen_cmd' term.
  2. **"Advanced" does not mean numerically larger** -- the sum is taken modulo 2^32, so wraparound is possible, and it is not guaranteed that `C != P'.
  3. *** MY EARLY-EXIT CLAIM WAS WRONG. ***  I wrote that after an aborted transfer the field holds *the PROGRAMMED address*.  It holds the **ENTRY value**, which may itself be a PREVIOUS transfer's cursor -- an early return preserves what was there, it does not restore a separately retained programmed address.  Also the `!d->enable' check comes FIRST, so a disabled AND unaligned address takes the disabled return and never reaches the alignment diagnostic.

WRITERS OF THE FIELD, complete for these two files: structure initialisation, the register write arm, and the DMA completion assignment.  Neither reset register clears it (`MAPLE_RESET' clears `enable'), and the tick function touches input queues only.  **The cursor is published at the TAIL, not incrementally**, and the ordinary trigger is SYNCHRONOUS -- writing 1 to `MAPLE_STATE' calls the transfer routine directly, with no scheduled DMA worker -- so no partially-advanced value can be observed.  *Scope caveat the seat raised itself: the routine calls `cpu->memory_rw', and these two files do not establish that such a callback can never re-enter device access.*

*** THE DETECTOR I PROPOSED IS INSUFFICIENT, AND THIS IS THE PART THAT CHANGES THE ROUND. ***
  * **Assertion (i), exact readback with no DMA, is passable by four wrong implementations:** a constant equal to the one test value; constant zero against an initial-zero-only test; ALIGNMENT MASKING against any test using only aligned values; and a separate snapshot of the last programmed address that never tracks DMA at all.  *Remedy: several distinct values, including nonzero HIGH bits and nonzero LOW FIVE bits, and successive writes shown to replace what reads report.  No DMA is needed for the unaligned cases.*
  * **Assertion (ii), post-transfer inequality, proves only that the answer differs from `P'** -- satisfied by zero, by a fabricated `P + 4', by a stale cursor from an earlier transfer, and by any masked transform that still differs.  Independent DMA evidence rules out a SKIPPED transfer; it says nothing about the relationship between the returned value and the field.
  * **THE FORM THAT WORKS:** capture the actual field value `S' immediately before the read, then assert the delivered register value equals `S' EXACTLY, that the read leaves the field unchanged, and that the access returns normally with NO read-side diagnostic.  Apply it both after ordinary programming and after an independently demonstrated transfer.
  * *** `MAPLE_STATE == 0' IS NOT DMA EVIDENCE: its read arm always returns zero, including after an early return. ***  Use a supported command and verify a fresh expected response in a receive buffer pre-filled with distinguishable contents; a completion event alone is weaker, because the descriptor loop can reach the tail through paths that do not implement the request fully.
  * **Candidate (c) -- keep `fatal()' and delete only `exit(1)' -- is NOT rejected by any value assertion if `fatal()' returns.  Silence and normal completion must be checked separately.**

PARTITION OF THE CHANGE, exact: only `relative_addr == 0x04' in the non-write branch moves.  The changed read class includes EVERY field value and history -- initial zero, freshly programmed values, UNALIGNED values, completed-DMA cursors, values preserved by disabled or unaligned attempts, and values retained across reset writes -- with no enable or alignment condition on the corrected read.  *A syntactic subtlety worth a row's comment: the `else' also covers a direction flag equal to neither MEM_WRITE nor MEM_READ, which previously terminated and afterwards assigns `odata' and returns without serialising it.*

Attachment is unconditional at `machine_dreamcast.c:149', BEFORE the `prom_emulation' early return.

rows.title: cpu_arm_coproc.c arm_coproc_i80321_6: reading the modelled XScale CP6 interrupt-enable register loads the correct value into rd and then calls exit(1) -- while the ADJACENT case 4 reads its own modelled register with no fatal and no exit
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10 from the GPT-6 Astra exit audit (regress/artifacts/queuetriage/codex_exitaudit_20260910.txt), which ranked it I1/E1. VERIFIED LOCALLY by opening the file before filing.

In `arm_coproc_i80321_6', crm 0 / crn 0, the load arm reads:
    cpu->cd.arm.r[rd] = cpu->cd.arm.i80321_inten;
    fatal("TODO: XScale read from inten?\n");
    exit(1);
The destination register receives the modelled value and the process then dies.  The STORE arm immediately below writes the same field, and the i80321 interrupt controller consumes it, so the register is fully modelled in both directions.

*** THE DECISIVE EVIDENCE IS THE SIBLING CASE IN THE SAME SWITCH, and it is one screen away: `case 4:' (i80321_isteer) has the IDENTICAL structure -- load arm assigns `cpu->cd.arm.r[rd] = cpu->cd.arm.i80321_isteer;', store arm writes it -- and carries NO fatal() and NO exit(). ***  So crn 0's kill is an OUTLIER inside its own switch rather than a policy, which is the upstream-residue pattern this project has now found several times: the author hit the exit he happened to reach while developing, and the sibling he did not.  That is a far stronger warrant than 'it is a host kill', and it is one grep away -- exactly what the option-set rule's sibling check is for.

REACHABILITY: machine_iq80321.c installs it explicitly (`cpu->cd.arm.coproc[6] = arm_coproc_i80321_6;'), and Iyonix does the same.  This is not an unattached helper. Emulated firmware reading its own interrupt-enable register is the natural consumer, and the generic coprocessor dispatcher enforces no supervisor-only precondition of its own.

DISPOSITION: option-set member 4 (ACCEPT) -- delete the two lines, keep the assignment, with NO latch, for the same reason as [[mapledmaaddr]]: the read is implemented and is not ignored, so an announce would ship a wrong record.  FAULT is unavailable here in any case: memory_rw.c delivers a failed-device exception for MIPS and M88K only, and this is ARM.

NOT MEASURED and no witness built; the rung-3 attempt is owed.  Note a witness needs a coprocessor read from an ARM guest, which is a different vehicle from the device probes this project mostly writes -- gate_arm.sh's 358 decode checks are the nearest existing machinery.

*** DESIGN REVIEW 2026-09-10: ACCEPT IS RATIFIED, BUT MY SIBLING WARRANT WAS OVERCLAIMED AND IS NARROWED HERE.  Verified locally before recording. ***

I wrote that the adjacent `case 4:' (isteer) 'carries NO fatal() and NO exit()'.  **FALSE ABOUT THE WHOLE CASE.**  Its READ arm is quiet, as I said -- but its STORE arm assigns the field and then `exit(1)' on ANY NONZERO VALUE.

**THE ASYMMETRY I RELIED ON SURVIVES, AND ONLY IN THE READ DIRECTION:** case 4 READS quietly while case 0 READS and dies, which is the outlier evidence.  In the WRITE direction the two swap over -- case 0 writes quietly, case 4 writes and dies on nonzero.  So the file has kills in both cases, on opposite halves, and the correct statement is that THE READ HALVES ARE ASYMMETRIC, not that one case is clean and the other is not.

The verdict stands with a narrower warrant: **ACCEPT for the ordinary interrupt-enable read into a general register.**  Its sibling's write-side kill is a SEPARATE defect on a separate arm and belongs to a separate row, not folded into this one.

*** THE OTHER SEVEN EXITS IN THIS FILE ARE TRIAGED, 2026-09-10 (xscaleinten/codex_coproc_20260910.txt, ZERO cyber flags) -- AND MY WORKING HYPOTHESIS IS REFUTED. ***

I asked which of the other seven share this row's shape, on the theory that 'the value is already computed and then discarded' would make several of them one cheap round.  **NONE OF THE OTHER SEVEN HAS THE SAME WARRANTED TWO-LINE ACCEPT REPAIR.**  That is a useful negative: it stops a round copying this disposition across the file, which is exactly what the option-set rule warns about when a precedent is transferred without checking each site.

**AND THE CENSUS UNDERCOUNTED THE FILE: eight ACTIVE exits plus SIX COMMENTED-OUT ones.**  The commented six are inert and are not defects, but they are worth knowing about -- a round de-fatalising a live site sits beside six places where someone already made that call and left the corpse in.

THE STRUCTURE, which is what decides how the remaining seven split into rounds: three CP15 sites, four CP6, one CP14 -- or by SHAPE, five specific-case sites, TWO DEFAULT-FED ENDPOINTS and one ENTRY GUARD.  The two default-fed ones are the priorities: CP6's shared `unknown:' label is reached from THREE defaults (the outer crm switch and both nested crn switches) and CP14's from FOUR plus a separate opcode2 guard -- so one repair at each label covers many decode paths at once.

*** ONE SITE IS NEITHER A CASE NOR A DEFAULT, which no other exit in this queue has been: CP15's `rd == ARM_PC' ENTRY GUARD, before the switch, in BOTH directions. ***  A refusal that fires before any dispatch is a different fix shape from every other member of this class, and it is ranked last for that reason rather than because it is unimportant.

*** REACHABILITY ANSWERED **YES** 2026-09-10 (xscaleinten/codex_witness_20260910.txt, GPT-6 Astra at max, ZERO cyber flags), AND MY NEGATIVE PREMISE WAS FALSE.  This row now has a ratified disposition, a confirmed path, and a named vehicle -- it needs a measuring seat and nothing else. ***

**INSTALLERS: exactly two, and both assign BEFORE the `!machine->prom_emulation' early return**, so disabling PROM emulation does not remove CP6 -- `machine_iq80321.c' (default CPU `80321_600_2') and `machine_iyonix.c' (`80321_600_B0'), each a direct `cpu->cd.arm.coproc[6] = ...'.  No other installer or caller exists.  **Selecting an XScale CPU is NOT enough**: generic ARM init installs CP15 and, for XScale, CP14 -- never CP6.  Note the setup receives the BOOTSTRAP cpu only.

**PATH:** guest fetch -> `arm_instr_to_be_translated' -> condition-selected `arm_instr_mcr_mrc' -> `arm_mcr_mrc' -> `coproc[6]' -> this handler.  **No privilege or mode check anywhere in that chain** -- dispatch does not consult CPAR (stored and read through CP15, and the source says it is otherwise unused).  Cold init already selects SVC32 with IRQ/FIQ masked, so no privilege transition is needed.  Prerequisites are ordinary: the condition must pass, the fetch must succeed, ARM state not Thumb, and CP6 must be installed -- with a null entry `arm_mcr_mrc' prints a generic TODO and **its undefined-exception call and `exit(1)' are COMMENTED OUT**, so absence does not terminate.

*** MY NEGATIVE PREMISE -- 'the machinery is store/load-oriented and nothing drives a coprocessor transfer' -- IS MEASURABLY FALSE. ***  FIVE existing probes already execute CP15 MRC/MCR on `cats': `footbridge_sites_probe.py', `fbpending_witness.py', `fbpending_drain_probe.py', `pit8253_latch_probe.py', and gate 14's `arm_flags_probe.py' on `testarm'.  **The directly reusable pattern is `footbridge_sites_probe.py'** -- launch a stock machine into the debugger, plant instructions in RAM, set pc, step, check disassembly, inspect registers -- pointed at IQ80321 or Iyonix instead of `cats'.  **No machine or device addition is required**, which is what the witness ladder demands.  No dedicated CP6 test exists yet.

*** AN ORACLE TRAP THAT APPLIES FAR BEYOND THIS ROW: A PRINTED STEP DISASSEMBLY DOES NOT PROVE THE INSTRUCTION EXECUTED, OR EVEN THAT ITS CONDITION PASSED.  The engine prints the disassembly BEFORE executing. ***  Any probe here that treats a stepped disassembly line as evidence of execution is asserting something the engine does not promise.

**A NAIVE `write W, read, expect W' HAS FOUR INDISTINGUISHABLE FAILURES:** always-zero (passes when `W' is zero); a stale value equal to `W'; a read that never executes (passes when the destination already holds `W' -- *especially easy if the write-source register is reused as the read destination*); and a program that never ran at all, when the inspected register or memory already holds the expected value.  **The discriminating form:** two DISTINCT NONZERO values written and read in succession, the read destination deliberately pre-set to a third value before each read, and SEPARATE write-source and read-destination registers.  Plus execution evidence -- intended address, decoded coprocessor and register fields, the destination TRANSITION, and continuation -- with missing observations failing rather than defaulting to zero.

**AND THE ORACLE NEEDS CONTINUATION AND SILENCE, not just a value:** the CURRENT code already assigns the destination before terminating, so the assignment alone is not the outcome under test.  Unchanged source predicts the named diagnostic and exit status 1; the corrected behaviour requires the right value, continued execution, and NO diagnostic from this read arm.

**THE SAME VEHICLE REACHES EVERY OTHER TERMINATION IN THIS FUNCTION** -- interrupt steering (`crn=4', write, nonzero), interrupt acknowledge (`crn=8', write, ANY value including zero), and the shared `unknown:' label (either direction, unsupported `crn' or `crm').  `opcode1' and `opcode2' are NOT validated, so changing them alone does not route a recognised selection to `unknown'.  *** EACH SITE NEEDS ITS OWN PROCESS INVOCATION, because the first `exit(1)' reached prevents observing any later one. ***  That groups the COVERAGE work without implying the repairs should be identical.

**A COUNT IN MY OWN BRIEF WAS WRONG: `crm=1' has SIXTEEN implemented direction arms -- eight reads and eight writes -- not fourteen.**  All sixteen are locally quiet, but *** 'quiet' DOES NOT MEAN 'a plain storage assignment' ***: `tcr0' and `tcr1' INCREMENT before returning their values, and a `tisr' write clears selected bits and deasserts timer interrupts.  A sibling-parity argument resting on 'the timer arms are plain accessors' would be wrong.

rows.title: dev_sgi_ip32.c DEVICE_ACCESS(crime): any access whose length is not 4 or 8 falls to `fatal("crime access len = %i!"); exit(1)', so ONE guest byte or halfword load to the IP32 memory/interrupt controller ends the emulator -- and this is MIPS, where the FAULT member is actually available
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10 from the GPT-6 Astra exit audit (regress/artifacts/queuetriage/codex_exitaudit_20260910.txt), which listed it among the six E1 predicates.  VERIFIED LOCALLY by opening the file.

The handler is a bare `if (len == 8) {...} else if (len == 4) {...} else { fatal(...); exit(1); }'.  There is no other width arm, so EVERY other access length -- 1, 2, and anything wider -- reaches the kill.  A byte load is an ordinary thing for a guest or a PROM to do while probing, and nothing about the device's mapping advertises a width restriction.

REACHABILITY: machine_sgi.c installs it with `dev_crime_init(machine, mem, 0x14000000, ...)' on the IP32 machines.  CRIME is the memory and interrupt controller, i.e. one of the first things any IP32 guest touches.

*** THE DISPOSITION IS THE INTERESTING PART, because member 5 (FAULT) IS GENUINELY AVAILABLE HERE, which it usually is not. ***  memory_rw.c converts a failed device callback into an architectural access exception for MIPS and M88K only -- and this device is on MIPS.  So `return 0' is not a silent decline here: it is a positive statement that the access could not be serviced, delivered to the guest as the bus error real hardware would give.  That is the dev_unreadable.c idiom the option set records, and machine_sgi.c already installs dev_unreadable ten times for exactly this reason -- the PROM and NetBSD probe absent regions and RELY on the failure.  A round here should weigh FAULT against DECLINE rather than defaulting to decline as most of this queue does.

NOT MEASURED, no witness.  The rung-3 attempt is owed and looks cheap: an IP32 machine with a single byte load at 0x14000000 through the debugger.

*** DESIGN REVIEW 2026-09-10 (faultpair/codex_faultpair_20260910.txt): THE VERDICT GOES AGAINST MY LEANING -- DECLINE + LATCHED ANNOUNCE, **NOT** FAULT -- and the distinction is the useful part. ***

I filed this row arguing that FAULT is available here and should be weighed first.  The review agrees it is MECHANICALLY available and rules against using it anyway: *'the evidence does not justify treating either entire refusal predicate as a hardware bus-error condition.'*  **AVAILABLE IS NOT THE SAME AS RIGHT.**  dev_unreadable.c's precedent is about a positively ABSENT device, and this is a PRESENT device refusing one access width -- returning a machine check for a width the model simply has not implemented asserts something about the hardware that nothing here establishes.

*** AND MY REACHABILITY STORY WAS TOO NARROW, which sharpens the row rather than weakening it. ***  I wrote 'any len that is not 4 or 8'.  The review establishes the population properly: ordinary MIPS scalar accesses deliver 1, 2, 4 or 8 bytes, and the load/store handler checks ALIGNMENT before calling memory_rw -- **which does not exclude byte accesses or aligned halfwords**, so 1 and 2 are ordinary guest traffic.  The unaligned left/right instructions use aligned 4- or 8-byte transactions and do NOT manufacture odd callback lengths.  **But EIGHT BYTES IS NOT A GLOBAL CALLBACK MAXIMUM:** IP32 also installs MEC, whose transmit-descriptor reader passes a THIRTY-TWO-BYTE buffer through physical memory_rw, and that path is not restricted to RAM.  So wider CRIME callbacks cannot be recorded as dead on the strength of scalar instruction widths, and `len' is a size_t rather than an unconstrained guest integer but is not universally {1,2,4,8} either.

So the round is a DECLINE with a latched announce, and its detector must cover BOTH the small widths (ordinary scalar traffic) and at least one wide callback (the descriptor path).

*** THE PREMISE I CALLED MY LEAST CERTAIN IS SETTLED, BY READING TWO LINES -- AND THE READING SEAT REFUSED THE QUESTION TWICE.  2026-09-10. ***

**`memory_rw.c` PASSES THE GUEST'S ACCESS WIDTH TO THE DEVICE CALLBACK UNCHANGED:**

        res = mem->devices[i].f(cpu, mem, paddr,
            data, len, writeflag,
            mem->devices[i].extra);

There is no widening, splitting or alignment at that call site, so a guest one-byte load arrives at `DEVICE_ACCESS(crime)' with `len == 1', falls past both width arms and reaches the terminating call.  **The route is confirmed by construction of the dispatcher, not by a measurement** -- what is still owed is the rung-3 witness that actually drives it.

*** TWO CODEX REFUSALS ON THIS ONE SUBJECT, AND THE SECOND KILLED MY OWN EXPLANATION OF THE FIRST. ***  Run 1 was refused with the whole-`regress` scope and a question asking for a census of terminating calls across the file; I hypothesised the census ask was the trigger.  Run 2 dropped the census question AND narrowed the scope to five named files -- **refused again, in the same place, with ZERO `regress/artifacts` hits.**

The log says what it was doing: reading **`memory_rw.c`** when the flag fired, 45 termination tokens in its own reasoning, none from an archive.  **The reading that survives the pair is that asking a seat to TRACE A GUEST-CHOSEN INPUT THROUGH THE MEMORY DISPATCHER TO A HOST-TERMINATION SITE is the trigger** -- with [[xscaleinten]] as the near-control, since it asked the same can-an-ordinary-instruction-reach-this question, in the same session, with the same scoping paragraph, and came back clean because its path runs through a handler TABLE rather than through memory dispatch.

*** SO THIS QUESTION IS NOT CODEX'S, AND IT COST TWO INVOCATIONS TO LEARN. ***  A width-reachability trace is something a MEASURING seat settles by measuring -- drive the byte load on an unmodified IP32 machine and see -- faster than a reading seat takes to refuse it.  **DO NOT RE-FIRE A THIRD TIME**: two refusals on two differently-worded briefs is a seat declining the SUBJECT, and the re-fire-once rule is about WALLS, not refusals.  Both refusal logs are preserved.

WHAT THE ROW NEEDS NOW, in order: a rung-3 witness on an unmodified IP32 machine (one guest byte load at `0x14000000` through the debugger), then the ratified repair -- decline the unsupported width with a bounded latched announce -- then a detector whose oracle separates a correct decline from (a) a handler answering zero at every width, (b) one that quietly services the byte against the wrong register, and (c) a run where the access never happened.  **A bare 'the emulator kept running' assertion sees none of those three**, which is the survive-only vacuity this project has measured before.

rows.title: dev_vme.c: the default arm announces with debug() -- INVISIBLE at default verbosity -- and then calls exit(1), so a guest probing an unimplemented VME2 register kills the emulator with NO VISIBLE REASON; M88K, so the FAULT member is available
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10 from the GPT-6 Astra exit audit, listed among the six E1 predicates. VERIFIED LOCALLY.

*** THIS ONE IS WORSE THAN THE USUAL SHAPE AND THE REASON IS THE DIAGNOSTIC LEVEL. ***  Every other unimplemented-register kill in this queue announces with `fatal()', which this fork has measured CANNOT be silenced by -q (debugmsg.c: fatal() has no early-out and goes straight to va_debug).  This one uses **debug()**, which DOES have an early-out -- `if ((quiet_mode && !ss) || v < 0) return;' -- so at default verbosity the message is not printed at all.  **The emulator therefore dies with no output explaining why.**  A user sees the process vanish; a gate sees a non-zero exit and no diagnostic to grep.  That makes this the hardest member of the class to DIAGNOSE, independent of how hard it is to trigger.

REACHABILITY: machine_mvme88k.c installs it -- `vme addr=0x%x', VME2_BASE -- unconditionally on a machine this project actively boots (the same constructor attaches the PCC2 the recent rounds are about).  Probing a bus controller's register space is exactly what firmware does.

DISPOSITION: member 5 (FAULT) is AVAILABLE -- M88K is one of the two families for which memory_rw.c delivers a failed-device exception -- so `return 0' gives the guest the bus error real VME hardware would.  Member 3 (decline + latched announce) is the alternative and would need the announce PROMOTED from debug() to fatal() to be worth anything, which is a second change the round must make deliberately rather than inherit.

NOT MEASURED, no witness; the rung-3 attempt is owed.

*** DESIGN REVIEW 2026-09-10: DECLINE + LATCHED ANNOUNCE, and the review RATIFIES PROMOTING THE DIAGNOSTIC -- 'including deliberate promotion of its default-arm diagnostics to fatal()'. ***  So the second change this row flagged is not an optional rider; it is part of the disposition.  FAULT is mechanically available on M88K and is ruled OUT for the same reason as [[crimewidthkill]]: this is a PRESENT device refusing an unimplemented register, not an absent one, and a bus error would assert something about the hardware that nothing establishes.

REACHABILITY CONFIRMED AND MADE PRECISE: the registered aperture is 4 KiB while the exact-offset switch recognises only TEN offsets, and the device's own vendored header names further real registers -- the second timer, interrupt status, master mapping controls -- that have NO cases at all.  So both reads and writes reach the default arm through ordinary register access, not through anything exotic.

rows.title: dev_fbctrl.c: the PORT arm ACCEPTS an out-of-range port number with a warning and STORES it, and the DATA arm then calls exit(1) on that same stored value -- a two-step, guest-driven host kill where the first step looks handled
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10 from the GPT-6 Astra exit audit, listed among the six E1 predicates. VERIFIED LOCALLY, and the local reading found a SHARPER SHAPE than the audit described.

*** THE TWO STEPS, and the first is what makes this nasty. ***
  case DEV_FBCTRL_PORT (write):  d->current_port = idata;
                                 if (idata >= DEV_FBCTRL_NPORTS)
                                         fatal("[ WARNING: fbctrl port number is out of range! ]");
  case DEV_FBCTRL_DATA:          if (d->current_port < 0 || d->current_port >= DEV_FBCTRL_NPORTS) {
                                         fatal(...); exit(1); }
**The PORT arm stores the bad value FIRST and warns SECOND -- it does not reject it.**  So the model accepts an out-of-range selector, says WARNING, carries on, and then kills the host the moment the guest uses the selector it just accepted.  A reader auditing the PORT arm sees a range check and a diagnostic and concludes the case is handled; the check does nothing but print.

*** AND THE ORDER IS THE FIX'S FIRST QUESTION: refusing the store in the PORT arm closes the DATA kill without touching the DATA arm at all. ***  That is one line moved, and it makes the DATA guard the belt-and-braces it reads as.  The alternative -- declining at DATA -- leaves the model holding a selector it has agreed to and cannot use.

*** AND THE TWO GUARDS TEST DIFFERENT QUANTITIES, which is the guard-field/body-field discriminator the pre-table check mandates. ***  The PORT arm tests **`idata`**, a `uint64_t`; the DATA arm tests **`d->current_port`**, an `int` (verified in the struct).  The store between them TRUNCATES.  Both halves of the DATA guard are therefore live and neither is dead code: a guest writing 0xffffffff warns at PORT and lands `current_port == -1', killing via the `< 0' half; a guest writing 0x100000000 warns at PORT and truncates to a PERFECTLY VALID 0, so the warning fires about a value that turns out fine.  **The warning and the kill are keyed to different numbers**, so neither predicts the other, and a detector must not assume the warning marks the killing set.

REACHABILITY: machine_test.c attaches fbctrl at TWO sites, so it is on the `testmips' and `testarm' machines -- **the machines this project's own gates drive**, including the 358 decode checks in gate_arm.sh.  The device is a GXemul-specific test framebuffer controller, so a guest writing a port number is its ordinary use.

THIRD KILL IN THE SAME FILE, recorded so a round does not close on one: `fbctrl_command()' has `default: fatal("fbctrl_command: Unimplemented command %i."); exit(1);', reached by writing a command byte to the COMMAND port -- a THIRD guest-driven exit, and the audit ranked that one I2/separate because a command needs a defined outcome rather than a decline.  The DEVICE_ACCESS default arm is a fourth.

NOT MEASURED, no witness; the rung-3 attempt is owed and is cheaper here than anywhere else in this batch, because the test machines are already driven by existing probes.

*** DESIGN REVIEW 2026-09-10 (fbctrlportkill/codex_design_20260910.txt, GPT-6 Astra at max, ZERO cyber flags): REVISE -- decline + latched announce -- AND IT CORRECTED TWO OF MY PREMISES. ***

**MY 'THE FIX'S FIRST QUESTION IS ORDER' IS IMPRECISE, AND A SIMPLE REORDER IS INSUFFICIENT.**  In the seat's words: *'Their textual order does not cause the defect; storing before validation does.'*  The two case arms' order is irrelevant -- what is wrong is that the PORT arm assigns and THEN checks.  So the repair is not to swap two lines but to **move the assignment into the valid-value `else' of the range check**, add a per-instance `warned_bad_port' latch for the announce, and leave the DATA arm untouched.  My framing would have produced a smaller edit that does not close it.

**AND THE TRUNCATION PREMISE NEEDED A WARRANT I DID NOT GIVE.**  I argued the `< 0' half is live because the field is a signed `int'.  The seat: *'signed int alone does not prove the conversion result'* -- C99 permits an implementation-defined result or a signal when converting an unrepresentable value to a signed type.  **The conclusion survives on the compiler's documented contract**: GCC documents reduction modulo the destination width, and under that contract both worked examples hold and the negative half IS live.  The unsigned input declaration does not make it dead.  *A true claim resting on an unstated assumption is exactly what the premise-audit clause exists to surface.*

**THE DEVICE IS ON MORE MACHINES THAN I WROTE.**  I said `testmips' and `testarm'.  The shared setup site also serves **testm88k, testppc, testriscv and testsh** -- so the blast radius is every test machine in the tree, not two of them.

CONFIRMED AS FILED: the PORT arm assigns before it checks; the selector is a plain `int'; a guest can read the stored selector back through the PORT arm, which gives a detector a channel that is NOT survive-only; and `fatal()' by itself does not terminate -- only the explicit `exit(1)' does.

*** A FLOOR NOTE THE ROUND MUST CARRY: 'a verbatim reinstatement of the removed kill' is INCOMPATIBLE with a repair that RETAINS that kill. ***  This disposition leaves the DATA arm's `exit(1)' in place as belt-and-braces, so there is nothing removed to reinstate.  The same shape as #521, where the fix made a kill unreachable rather than deleting it -- and the same answer: name the distinguishable mutant (restoring the store-before-validate order) rather than pretending the literal clause is met.

rows.title: THE UNOWNED REMAINDER: 76 guest-reachable error-exit sites across 24 files own no tracker row -- a TRACKING row so the body of work has a denominator and a pointer, not a re-derivation
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10.  Evidence: regress/artifacts/queuetriage/codex_exitaudit_20260910.txt (GPT-6 Astra at max), which enumerated the population properly for the first time.  **This row exists so the next session reads the census instead of re-running it**, which has now happened twice.

*** THE EARLIER FIGURES WERE RIGHT AND THEIR DESCRIPTION WAS WRONG: 370 and 240 count `exit(1)', NOT every `exit()'. ***  Re-derived by removing comments and string literals while preserving line positions, then locating the calls, with an independent character-state lexer returning exactly the same positions:

    src/devices    263 literal `exit('   135 calls after lexical filtering
    src/cpus       112                    74
    src/machines    35                    34
    TOTAL          410                   243   (240 of them exit(1))

LOCATION SPLIT of those 243: 150 runtime handlers and helpers, 80 init/configuration, 13 CPU generators and a standalone experiment.  The debugger is outside that scope and adds three more.

AND BEING INSIDE A RUNTIME FUNCTION IS NOT REACHABILITY.  The 150 split: **98 input-reachable through enabled in-tree wiring**; 33 dead, precluded, or not established reachable; 10 optional instrumentation; 6 unattached or disabled attachments; 2 intentional halt/reboot; 1 host RAM-config check misplaced in an access handler.

OWNERSHIP is an OVERLAY, not a disjoint population -- 22 live exits and 3 others are actively owned (n6 holds eight footbridge sites; alphavmkill one; sgirekills five; lcaisalane and lcabadval eight between them; m88kexit two dead ones).  **A strict open/held filter leaves 83, of which seven belong to in-work LCA repairs, so THE UNOWNED REMAINDER IS 76.**

*** AND ONE OF MY OWN EARLIER QUALIFICATIONS WAS TOO AGGRESSIVE, corrected here: lacking a separate CHILD repair id does not mean lacking an open OWNING row.  `sgirekills' explicitly retains its five command exits.  Conversely an incidental mention in census prose is NOT a repair row. ***

SIX E1 PREDICATES were identified -- a one-to-five-line change with an existing test carrier -- and ALL SIX ARE NOW FILED as their own rows: [[mk48nvramkill]], [[mapledmaaddr]], [[xscaleinten]], [[crimewidthkill]], [[vmedefaultkill]], [[fbctrlportkill]].  **This row therefore tracks the ~70 that remain, and they are E2/E3: real rounds, not quick wins.**  The heaviest concentrations are dev_osiop.c (14), cpu_arm_coproc.c (8 of which one is filed), dev_adb.c (7), dev_dreamcast_g2.c (6), dev_pvr.c and dev_igsfb.c (5 each).

THE ONE CONSTRAINT THAT GOVERNS EVERY DISPOSITION IN THIS BODY, and it is easy to forget: **memory_rw.c turns a failed device callback into an architectural access exception for MIPS and M88K ONLY.**  Returning zero from an ARM or SH device callback gives NO bus-error delivery, so the FAULT member is unavailable there and a round reaching for it owes the exception path first.  CPU translation and instruction handlers have their own direct mechanisms, which is a separate question.

*** THE LARGEST CONCENTRATION HAS BEEN TRIAGED, 2026-09-10: dev_osiop.c (osiopexits/codex_triage_20260910.txt, GPT-6 Astra at max; 3 cyber flags, ALL MID-STREAM and non-fatal). ***

**THE FILE HAS SIXTEEN EXPLICIT exit() CALLS, NOT FOURTEEN.**  The census's fourteen are all still executable, and two more exist that it did not list -- **and those two are the ones that turn out to be DEAD**, so the census happened to enumerate exactly the live set without saying why.

    (i)   guest register access or guest-started SCRIPTS      **14**  -- one register default,
                                                                        thirteen sequencer exits
    (ii)  unconstructible state or impossible branch          **2**
    (iii) internal failures where stopping is right           **0**

*** POPULATION (iii) BEING EMPTY IS ITSELF THE FINDING, and it is the one that licenses the whole body of work.  NONE of the sixteen checks establishes corrupted host ownership or any other condition that requires terminating.  The seat says the diagnostic wording -- notably 'cannot be combined' -- does NOT turn these into internal assertions, which is the argument a round would otherwise have to make sixteen times. ***

THE TWO DEAD PATHS, RECORDED WITH THEIR WARRANTS so nobody re-finds them:
  * the reserved-phase MOVE default -- an earlier equality check forces the instruction phase to match SOCL; initialisation and every implemented transition produce only handled phases; SET/CLEAR do not touch the phase bits; and a direct SOCL write terminates at the REGISTER DEFAULT before another SCRIPTS execution can run.  *That last clause is why this one is dead only while the register default is still fatal -- fixing the register default could REVIVE it, which a round must not miss.*
  * the outer instruction-class default is **mathematically unreachable**: the switch evaluates `dcmd & 0xc0' and explicitly handles all four possible results.

**AND IT CORRECTED THE AUDIT'S EFFORT RANKING:** the blanket E3 (`preserve command termination, status and interrupt behaviour') OVERSTATES the obligation for the register default and the redundant table-MOVE equality check, because the real status and completion sequence lives in the STATUS and MSG_IN phases, and the backend-failure branches are ALREADY de-fatalised by earlier rounds and sit outside this census.  So two of the nine prescribed rows are cheaper than the audit implied.

*** THE SEVERITY CEILING, ASKED FOR AND ANSWERED PLAINLY: 'no in-tree runnable workload drives this controller's register/SCRIPTS interface.' ***  All fourteen are guest-reachable in principle and NOTHING IN THIS TREE EXERCISES THEM.  That is worth more than a ranking: it means these rounds cannot reach rung 4, and a witness must plant SCRIPTS by hand.

A TRAP NAMED FOR THE FIRST ROW, and it is the kind that makes a one-line repair wrong: the generic byte path STORES BEFORE DISPATCH, and the word path also stores to DNAD and ADDER before reaching the unhandled-register default -- so restoring only `oldreg' would NOT undo those word stores.  And a blanket backed-accept would enable SOCL writes, **which changes the reserved-phase reachability finding above**.  The two interact.

NINE REPAIR ROWS PRESCRIBED covering the fourteen, in priority order: register default; redundant table-MOVE equality check; MOVE phase mismatch; transfer-control handling; MOVE addressing modes; SELECT validation; WAIT RESELECT; register/ALU instructions; MEMORY MOVE.  Not filed individually yet -- filing nine rows for a controller nothing drives would crowd a queue that already holds live guest-reachable kills on machines this project DOES boot.

rows.title: cpu_ppc_instr.c X(rldicl) ALWAYS WRITES ZERO: the mask is accumulated into `tmp' while the destination is assigned `tmp & tmp2' and tmp2 is never anything but 0 -- one of the most common 64-bit PowerPC instructions returns 0 for every input
rows.note:
FILED 2026-09-10.  Found by the GPT-6 Astra seat under the found-something-else licence while answering a tree-wide SHIFT-UB census -- it says so itself: *'one definite additional finding deserves its own correctness row ... This is CRITICAL and EASY, independently of the shift-UB census.'*  **VERIFIED LOCALLY by opening the handler before filing.**

*** THE DEFECT, and it is four lines you can hold in your head. ***
    uint64_t tmp = cpu->cd.ppc.gpr[rs], tmp2;
    while (sh-- != 0) { ... rotate tmp left by one ... }
    tmp2 = 0;
    while (mb <= 63) {
            tmp |= ((uint64_t)1 << (63-mb));      <-- the MASK goes into tmp
            mb ++;
    }
    cpu->cd.ppc.gpr[ra] = tmp & tmp2;             <-- tmp2 is STILL 0
`tmp2' is assigned 0 and never assigned again, so **the destination register is set to zero on every execution, for every operand, every rotate amount and every mask begin.**  The `|=' also corrupts the rotated value it lands in, but that is moot: the result is ANDed with zero either way.

*** THE SIBLING TWO FUNCTIONS DOWN SHOWS THE INTENDED SHAPE, which is what makes the diagnosis certain rather than inferred. ***  X(rldicr) does the same rotate and then CLEARS bits in `tmp' (`tmp &= ~((uint64_t)1 << (63-me))'), assigning `tmp' directly.  X(rldicl) was written the other way round -- BUILD a mask, then AND -- and the mask was accumulated into the wrong variable.  The fix is one character: `tmp |=' becomes `tmp2 |='.

*** WHY THIS IS THE MOST SERIOUS THING IN TODAY'S BATCH. ***  `rldicl' is not an obscure corner: it is THE canonical 64-bit PowerPC masking and zero-extension instruction, emitted constantly by compilers (`rldicl rA,rS,0,32' is the standard 32-bit zero-extend).  Every other defect filed today needs a guest to touch a particular register or width; this one is wrong on the ordinary path, for ordinary code, on every execution.

REACHABILITY IS WIRED AND CHECKED: `case PPC_30_RLDICL: ic->f = instr(rldicl); break;' in the primary decoder, reached whenever `cpu->cd.ppc.bits == 64' -- the 32-bit path deliberately goes to `bad' instead.  So it is live on every 64-bit PowerPC CPU model this tree offers, and dead on the 32-bit ones.

*** AND IT IS NOT A SHIFT DEFECT, which matters for how the round is scoped: the census explicitly records the computed count here as SAFE (mask counts 0..63, rotate counts 1..31, form NONE). *** This is a plain variable mix-up that the census found while looking at something else.  It does NOT belong to [[shiftubcensus]] or [[mipsextshift]]; it is its own correctness round.

NOT MEASURED and no witness built.  The rung-3 attempt is owed FIRST and looks unusually cheap: any 64-bit PowerPC machine, one `rldicl' with a nonzero source, and a register readback -- the wanted value is anything but zero, and the pre-fix build must show zero.  A guest-visible wrong RESULT is a far easier oracle than the process-death oracles most of this queue needs.  **Check first whether the existing PPC gates already execute one and pass anyway**, because a green gate over an always-zero instruction would itself be a finding about the gates.

*** WITNESSED AT RUNG 3, 2026-09-10, AND MY FILING UNDERSTATED IT IN THREE WAYS. ***

(a) **TWO TOKENS ARE WRONG, NOT ONE, AND THE OBVIOUS REPAIR WAS BUILT AND MEASURED STILL WRONG.**  The mask is ORed into `tmp', the ROTATED VALUE, so even setting the AND aside the data is destroyed by having every mask bit forced to 1.  `tmp2' never being written is a CONSEQUENCE of the same slip rather than an independent bug.  The seat built both candidates: the one-character `tmp |=' -> `tmp2 |=' measures CORRECT at 0 of 190 wrong, while DELETING the `& tmp2' -- the edit a future reader is most likely to reach for -- ships an OR where the architecture says AND and gets 126 of 190 cells wrong.  **It is worse than the present bug in one specific way: it removes the always-zero signature that makes the defect easy to spot while leaving the value wrong.**  Recorded so the next round does not take it.

(b) **A SECOND OBSERVABLE CHANNEL: IT CORRUPTS CONTROL FLOW, NOT ONLY DATA.**  update_cr0 is fed the destination, which is always zero, so the record form reports EQ on EVERY execution regardless of operands -- measured 0x20000000 committed against 0x40000000 fixed.  Any branch on a masked compare takes the wrong arm.  A detector owes a row on this channel.

(c) **IT IS REACHABLE ON A REAL MACHINE MODEL, not only a synthetic one.**  All three in-tree machines that select a 64-bit CPU return zero: bareppc, testppc, and macppc -e g5 -- the Power Mac G5, whose constructor gives it the PPC970.

THE ORACLE CAME FROM THE MANUAL, NOT FROM THIS TREE: the rldiclx RTL in ppc_pem_32and64_2005.txt plus its prose, with field placement taken from the manual's own format diagram and then independently confirmed by inverting the handler's extraction expressions.  Deriving the wants from the sibling would have been weaker and from the handler itself circular.  196 of 196 encoded words round-tripped through THE TREE'S OWN DISASSEMBLER, a different code path from the execute handler -- the defence against this project's hand-assembled-encoding trap, and it matters here because a wrong register field yields zero and zero is the symptom under test.

THE CENSUS IS NON-VACUOUS BY CONSTRUCTION, which is what makes 190 of 190 a real number: the source is all-ones, so the rotate is the identity and the architectural answer is exactly the mask, which is non-empty for every mask-begin in 0..63.  **And the seat measured a genuinely VACUOUS cell to show the boundary**: with a source whose selected window is all zeros the correct answer is itself zero and the row is GREEN on the broken build.  The rule for a detector author is to choose a source where every mask window is non-empty.

*** THE GATE FINDING IS STRUCTURAL AND STRONGER THAN 'NO GATE COVERS IT'. ***  Both PowerPC gates drive macppc -e g4, an MPC7400, which the CPU table marks 32-BIT -- and the decoder sends every rld* to the bad path in 32-bit mode.  **So no gate has ever instantiated a 64-bit PowerPC CPU at all, and the whole 64-bit-only instruction group is invisible to the gates BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by omission.**  That is better than a green gate passing over a broken instruction, which is what I had asked to be checked.  It is one coverage hole with one cause, and a single 64-bit probe closes all of it.

SEVERITY CEILING, stated honestly rather than glossed: the only PowerPC kernel image in the tree is loaded onto a G4 and never executed, so nothing in-tree BOOTS a 64-bit PowerPC guest.  The defect is catastrophic for any such guest and there is not currently one, which is why the witness is rung 3 and why it cannot be rung 4.

*** THE GATE CLAIM WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED HERE.  I WROTE IT INTO THREE ROWS, A CHANGELOG BLOCK AND TWO COMMIT MESSAGES BEFORE A SEAT CHECKED IT (wiringcliff/codex_ppcgate_20260910.txt). ***

**I CLAIMED: 'no gate in this tree instantiates a 64-bit PowerPC CPU at all, so the whole 64-bit-only instruction group is invisible BY CONSTRUCTION.'  THE FIRST HALF IS FALSE.**  Gate 9 (gate_asan_sweep.sh) enumerates EVERY advertised machine type and subtype -- including bareppc, testppc and macppc/g5, all of which default to the PPC970 -- so 64-bit PowerPC CPUs ARE constructed by a gate today, and have been all along.

**THE CORRECT AND NARROWER FINDING: NO GATE CHECKS THEIR INSTRUCTION RESULTS.**  Gate 9 is a CONSTRUCTION check with no PowerPC result oracle; the two PowerPC gates both drive `macppc -e g4', an MPC7400, which is 32-bit, and their probes select it EXPLICITLY rather than by default.  So the defects were invisible because nothing EXECUTES these instructions and inspects the answer -- not because nothing builds the CPU.

*** THAT DISTINCTION IS THIS PROJECT'S OWN WITNESS LADDER, ONE LEVEL UP, AND I WALKED PAST IT. ***  The ladder's whole rung-2 clause says machine CONSTRUCTION proves presence and NOT reachability, and is a reproduction only for defects that construction itself executes.  I applied that rule carefully to witnesses all day and then made exactly the error it warns about when reasoning about GATES.  A gate that constructs a CPU is a rung-2 gate; these defects need a rung-3 one.

THE PRESCRIBED CLOSURE IS SMALLER THAN MY FRAMING SUGGESTED: wire the existing 19-row regress/ppc_rldicl_probe.py into gate_ppc.sh, asserting its score AND its completion sentinel.  That closes the missing instruction-result check.  **It does NOT close all 64-bit PowerPC coverage**, and the seat says so explicitly rather than letting the round claim it does.

COMMITTED 19/27 with 190 of 190 census cells wrong and all 190 returning zero; FIX 24/27 with 0 of 190 wrong.  Logs witness_committed.out / witness_fix.out / witness_naive.out, each verified by its PPC_RLDICL_WITNESS_DONE sentinel.
